8.6 Density-based clustering
Centroid-based methods such as k-means define clusters by proximity to a representative center. This works well when groups are roughly spherical and have comparable spread, but it can fail when clusters have irregular shapes, different densities, or when the dataset contains outliers that should not belong to any cluster. Density-based clustering takes a different view: clusters are defined as contiguous regions of high point density separated by regions of low density.
In density-based clustering, a “good” cluster is not necessarily centered around a mean. Instead, a cluster is a connected set of observations where each observation lies in a neighborhood that contains “enough” nearby observations. This definition naturally supports non-spherical shapes (e.g., crescents, rings), and it provides an explicit mechanism to label observations that do not belong to any dense region as noise. In biomedical settings, this is often exactly what we want: unusual physiological episodes, artefacts, or rare phenotypes can be flagged rather than forced into a nearest-centroid group.
Two widely used density-based methods are DBSCAN and OPTICS. DBSCAN is the classic algorithm and introduces the key concepts (core points, border points, and noise). OPTICS generalizes DBSCAN to handle datasets where different clusters have different densities, and it provides a reachability plot that summarizes the cluster structure across scales.

# ===============================================================
# Density-based clustering setup
# - Simulated 2D examples (non-spherical shapes + noise)
# - Wearable dataset example (scaled features)
# ===============================================================
set.seed(2025)

# Helper: consistent theme
theme_set(theme_bw(base_size = 12))


8.6.1 DBSCAN: core points, border points, and noise
DBSCAN (Density-Based Spatial Clustering of Applications with Noise) defines clusters using two hyperparameters:

eps: the neighborhood radius ( \(\varepsilon\) )
minPts: the minimum number of points required to form a dense neighborhood

Given these two values, DBSCAN classifies observations into three types:

Core point: has at least minPts points (including itself) within distance eps.
Border point: has fewer than minPts neighbors within eps, but lies within eps of a core point.
Noise point: is neither a core point nor a border point.

The next chunk creates three small point clouds to illustrate DBSCAN’s local concept of density: a compact “dense region”, a looser “border region”, and scattered “noise”. It then selects a single candidate point in the dense region and draws its ε-neighborhood (a dashed circle of radius ε). In DBSCAN, whether a point becomes a core point depends on how many points fall inside this circle (including itself). The purpose of the figure is conceptual: it visually anchors the idea that clusters are grown from locally dense neighborhoods rather than around a global centroid.

# ===============================================================
# DBSCAN conceptual diagram with explicit epsilon (ε) — FIXED
# ===============================================================

library(tidyverse)

set.seed(1)

# Dense region
core_cluster <- tibble(
  x = rnorm(25, 0, 0.25),
  y = rnorm(25, 0, 0.25)
)

# Border-ish region
border_points <- tibble(
  x = rnorm(8, 0.8, 0.15),
  y = rnorm(8, 0.8, 0.15)
)

# Noise
noise_points <- tibble(
  x = runif(10, -2, 2),
  y = runif(10, -2, 2)
)

data_all <- bind_rows(
  core_cluster %>% mutate(type = "Dense region"),
  border_points %>% mutate(type = "Border region"),
  noise_points %>% mutate(type = "Noise")
)

# Candidate core point (example)
example_core <- core_cluster[1, ]

eps <- 0.5

# Epsilon circle
theta <- seq(0, 2*pi, length.out = 300)
circle <- tibble(
  x = example_core$x + eps * cos(theta),
  y = example_core$y + eps * sin(theta)
)

# Radius segment as a ONE-ROW tibble
radius_seg <- tibble(
  x    = example_core$x,
  y    = example_core$y,
  xend = example_core$x + eps,
  yend = example_core$y
)

ggplot(data_all, aes(x, y)) +
  geom_point(aes(color = type), size = 2.5, alpha = 0.85) +
  geom_path(
    data = circle, aes(x, y),
    linetype = "dashed", linewidth = 1.1, color = "black"
  ) +
  geom_segment(
    data = radius_seg,
    aes(x = x, y = y, xend = xend, yend = yend),
    linewidth = 1.1, color = "black"
  ) +
  annotate(
    "text",
    x = example_core$x + eps/2,
    y = example_core$y + 0.08,
    label = "\u03B5",  # Greek epsilon character
    size = 7
  ) +
  geom_point(
    data = example_core,
    aes(x, y),
    size = 4, color = "black"
  ) +
  coord_equal() +
  theme_bw(base_size = 13) +
  labs(
    title = "DBSCAN ε-Neighborhood Illustration",
    subtitle = "Dashed circle represents the ε-neighborhood around a candidate core point",
    color = NULL
  )








The figure above shows that clusters are formed by density connectivity: starting from a core point, DBSCAN expands a cluster by recursively adding all points that are within eps of any core point in the cluster. This expansion continues until no additional points can be added. Points that do not become part of any cluster are labelled as noise.
The key modeling idea is that DBSCAN does not “force” a partition. If an observation does not live in a sufficiently dense region, it is not assigned to a cluster.
The next example simulates a classic “non-convex” clustering geometry: two concentric rings plus uniform background noise. The chunk first plots the raw data to show that the structure is not well described by spherical, centroid-based groups. It then fits DBSCAN with chosen eps and minPts. DBSCAN assigns each point either to a cluster (positive integer label) or to cluster 0, which means “noise” (not density-connected to any core region). The final plot overlays this interpretation: points labelled as noise are shown in grey, while density-connected points are colored by cluster label. The purpose is to demonstrate DBSCAN’s two key advantages: (i) it can recover non-spherical structure, and (ii) it can explicitly leave outliers unassigned.

# ===============================================================
# Example 1: Rings + noise
# Three-panel comparison: raw data vs k-means vs DBSCAN
# Layout: ONE plot per row (3 rows total)
# Goal: DBSCAN recovers exactly TWO ring clusters + explicit noise
# ===============================================================

set.seed(2025)

# ---------------------------------------------------------------
# 1) Simulate two rings + uniform noise (clean geometry)
# ---------------------------------------------------------------
n_ring <- 350
t1 <- runif(n_ring, 0, 2*pi)
t2 <- runif(n_ring, 0, 2*pi)

# Slightly lower jitter -> more uniform local density along each ring
ring1 <- tibble(
  x = 1.0 * cos(t1) + rnorm(n_ring, 0, 0.05),
  y = 1.0 * sin(t1) + rnorm(n_ring, 0, 0.05)
)

ring2 <- tibble(
  x = 2.2 * cos(t2) + rnorm(n_ring, 0, 0.06),
  y = 2.2 * sin(t2) + rnorm(n_ring, 0, 0.06)
)

noise <- tibble(
  x = runif(140, -3, 3),
  y = runif(140, -3, 3)
)

toy_db <- bind_rows(
  ring1 %>% mutate(source = "ring1"),
  ring2 %>% mutate(source = "ring2"),
  noise %>% mutate(source = "noise")
)

# ---------------------------------------------------------------
# Plot 1: raw geometry (rings highlighted; noise faded)
# ---------------------------------------------------------------
p_raw <- ggplot(toy_db, aes(x, y)) +
  geom_point(
    data = subset(toy_db, source == "noise"),
    alpha = 0.20, size = 1.7, color = "grey75"
  ) +
  geom_point(
    data = subset(toy_db, source != "noise"),
    aes(color = source),
    alpha = 0.90, size = 1.7
  ) +
  coord_equal() +
  labs(
    title = "Toy data: two rings + uniform noise",
    subtitle = "Non-convex geometry (centroid-based methods struggle)",
    color = "Source"
  ) +
  theme_bw()

# ---------------------------------------------------------------
# Plot 2: k-means on the same data (k = 2)
# ---------------------------------------------------------------
km_fit <- kmeans(toy_db[, c("x", "y")], centers = 2, nstart = 20)

toy_km <- toy_db %>%
  mutate(km_cluster = factor(km_fit$cluster))

p_km <- ggplot(toy_km, aes(x, y, color = km_cluster)) +
  geom_point(alpha = 0.75, size = 1.7) +
  coord_equal() +
  labs(
    title = "k-means result (k = 2)",
    subtitle = "Centroid-based partition (often cuts across rings)",
    color = "Cluster"
  ) +
  theme_bw()

# ---------------------------------------------------------------
# Plot 3: DBSCAN (noise in grey, clusters in color)
# Choose eps so each ring stays density-connected as ONE cluster.
# ---------------------------------------------------------------
eps_use   <- 0.28
minPts_use <- 10 

db_fit <- dbscan::dbscan(toy_db[, c("x", "y")], eps = eps_use, minPts = minPts_use)

toy_db2 <- toy_db %>%
  mutate(
    cluster   = db_fit$cluster,     # numeric label; 0 = noise
    is_noise  = cluster == 0,
    cluster_f = factor(cluster)
  )

p_db <- ggplot(toy_db2, aes(x, y)) +
  geom_point(
    data = subset(toy_db2, is_noise),
    color = "grey60",
    alpha = 0.35,
    size = 1.7
  ) +
  geom_point(
    data = subset(toy_db2, !is_noise),
    aes(color = cluster_f),
    alpha = 0.90,
    size = 1.7
  ) +
  coord_equal() +
  labs(
    title = "DBSCAN result",
    subtitle = paste0("eps = ", eps_use, ", minPts = ", minPts_use, " (cluster 0 = noise)"),
    color = "Cluster"
  ) +
  theme_bw()

p_raw







p_km







p_db








The three figures presents three views of the same simulated dataset in order to contrast centroid-based and density-based clustering. The first plot shows the raw geometry: two concentric rings embedded in uniformly distributed background noise. This structure is non-convex, meaning that meaningful clusters follow curved manifolds rather than compact, spherical regions.
The second plot shows the result of applying k-means with k = 2. Because k-means minimizes within-cluster sum of squares, it prefers convex clusters separated by (approximately) linear boundaries in the feature space. On ring-shaped data, this tends to split the plane into two halves, cutting across both rings and mixing points that are close in Euclidean distance but belong to different parts of the same ring.
The third plot shows DBSCAN using a fixed ε (neighborhood radius) and minPts (minimum neighbors required for a dense region). DBSCAN labels points as either density-connected cluster members (positive integer labels) or noise (cluster 0). Here, the two rings are recovered as two coherent clusters because points remain connected through overlapping ε-neighborhoods along each ring, while isolated background points are left unassigned and appear in grey. This illustrates DBSCAN’s key advantage on non-convex structure: clusters are grown by local density connectivity, and outliers can be explicitly treated as noise rather than forced into a nearest-centroid partition.
The choice of ε directly controls the scale of density connectivity. If ε is too small, local gaps along a structure may break connectivity and fragment a single geometric object into multiple clusters. If ε is too large, distinct structures may merge and background noise may be absorbed into clusters.
The following illustration applies three different ε values to the same ring dataset while keeping minPts fixed.

# ===============================================================
# Sensitivity of DBSCAN to epsilon (ε)
# Same data, different ε values
# ===============================================================

# Keep minPts fixed
minPts_demo <- 10

# Three epsilon values
eps_small  <- 0.15   # Too small -> fragmentation
eps_good   <- 0.28   # Reasonable -> two rings recovered
eps_large  <- 0.55   # Too large -> merging + noise absorbed

run_dbscan_plot <- function(eps_value, title_text) {
  
  db_fit <- dbscan::dbscan(toy_db[, c("x", "y")],
                           eps = eps_value,
                           minPts = minPts_demo)
  
  toy_tmp <- toy_db %>%
    mutate(
      cluster   = db_fit$cluster,
      is_noise  = cluster == 0,
      cluster_f = factor(cluster)
    )
  
  ggplot(toy_tmp, aes(x, y)) +
    geom_point(
      data = subset(toy_tmp, is_noise),
      color = "grey60",
      alpha = 0.35,
      size = 1.5
    ) +
    geom_point(
      data = subset(toy_tmp, !is_noise),
      aes(color = cluster_f),
      alpha = 0.9,
      size = 1.5
    ) +
    coord_equal() +
    theme_bw(base_size = 12) +
    theme(legend.position = "none") +
    labs(
      title = title_text,
      subtitle = paste0("eps = ", eps_value,
                        ", minPts = ", minPts_demo)
    )
}

p_small <- run_dbscan_plot(eps_small,
                           "ε too small: ring fragments into multiple clusters")

p_good  <- run_dbscan_plot(eps_good,
                           "ε well calibrated: two rings recovered")

p_large <- run_dbscan_plot(eps_large,
                           "ε too large: clusters merge and noise is absorbed")

p_small







p_good







p_large










8.6.2 Choosing eps and minPts in practice
DBSCAN’s behavior is governed by eps and minPts, and these parameters must be chosen relative to the scale and dimensionality of the data. Two practical heuristics are commonly used:

Standardize features before clustering so that distances are comparable across variables.
Use a k-nearest-neighbor distance plot (kNN distance plot) to select eps.

The kNN distance plot works as follows. Fix minPts, and for each observation compute the distance to its k-th nearest neighbor (where \(\mathrm{k}=\) minPts). Sort these distances from smallest to largest and plot them. A typical “elbow” indicates a transition from points inside dense regions to points in sparse regions. Choosing eps near this elbow often yields a reasonable clustering.
The minPts parameter is often set to a small integer (e.g., 5-15) depending on sample size and expected cluster granularity. In higher dimensions, density becomes harder to estimate, and DBSCAN may require larger minPts or may become unstable. This is not a failure of implementation but a reflection of the curse of dimensionality: in high-dimensional spaces, distances become less informative and local neighborhoods become sparse.
The next chunk of code implements a practical heuristic for selecting eps. After fixing minPts, it computes, for every point, the distance to its k-th nearest neighbor (with k = minPts) and sorts these distances. Points inside dense regions tend to have small kNN distances; points in sparse regions (including noise) have larger kNN distances. The “elbow” in the sorted curve often marks a transition between these regimes, and choosing eps near that elbow typically yields a reasonable density threshold for DBSCAN.

# ===============================================================
# kNN distance plot for eps selection (heuristic)
# ===============================================================

minPts <- 8
knn <- dbscan::kNNdist(toy_db[, c("x", "y")], k = minPts)

knn_df <- tibble(
  idx = seq_along(knn),
  knn_dist = sort(knn)
)

ggplot(knn_df, aes(idx, knn_dist)) +
  geom_line(linewidth = 1) +
  geom_point(size = 1.5, alpha = 0.7) +
  labs(
    title = "kNN distance plot (eps selection heuristic)",
    subtitle = paste0("k = minPts = ", minPts, " (look for an elbow)"),
    x = "Sorted observations",
    y = paste0("Distance to the ", minPts, "-th nearest neighbor")
  )










8.6.3 Applying DBSCAN to the wearable dataset
In the wearable dataset, each observation corresponds to an individual summarized by a set of scaled physiological variables (resting heart rate, HRV, steps, skin temperature, oxygen saturation, and sleep efficiency). When applying DBSCAN here, we typically standardize all variables (as we already do for kmeans), and then run a kNN distance plot to choose an eps value.
The interpretation differs from k-means. DBSCAN may return: - a few dense physiological phenotypes (clusters), and - a set of “noise” observations that do not belong to any dense region
In a real remote-monitoring setting, these noise observations might correspond to unusual states (e.g., transient fever, sensor artefacts, or atypical recovery profiles). In a simulated dataset like ours, DBSCAN may or may not label a noise set depending on how separated and how dense the simulated groups are. This is not a bug; it is precisely the point of a density-based definition.

# ===============================================================
# DBSCAN on the wearable dataset (scaled features)
# ===============================================================

wear <- readRDS("~/att_ai_ml/att_book/data/wearable_cluster.rds")

wear_scaled <- wear %>%
  mutate(across(HR_mean:sleep_eff, ~ as.numeric(scale(.))))

X_wear <- as.matrix(wear_scaled %>% dplyr::select(HR_mean:sleep_eff))

minPts_wear <- 10
knn_wear <- dbscan::kNNdist(X_wear, k = minPts_wear)

knn_wear_df <- tibble(
  idx = seq_along(knn_wear),
  knn_dist = sort(knn_wear)
)

ggplot(knn_wear_df, aes(idx, knn_dist)) +
  geom_line(linewidth = 1) +
  geom_point(size = 1.2, alpha = 0.6) +
  labs(
    title = "Wearable data: kNN distance plot",
    subtitle = paste0("k = minPts = ", minPts_wear, " (choose eps near the elbow)"),
    x = "Sorted observations",
    y = paste0("Distance to the ", minPts_wear, "-th nearest neighbor")
  )







eps_wear <- 1.1
db_wear <- dbscan::dbscan(X_wear, eps = eps_wear, minPts = minPts_wear)

wear_db <- wear_scaled %>%
  mutate(
    db_cluster_num = db_wear$cluster,
    db_is_noise    = db_cluster_num == 0,
    db_cluster     = factor(db_cluster_num)
  )

table(wear_db$db_cluster)


  0   1   2   3   4 
 16 157 316 156 155 

ggplot(wear_db, aes(HR_mean, steps_mean)) +
  geom_point(
    data = subset(wear_db, db_is_noise),
    color = "grey60",
    alpha = 0.45,
    size = 2
  ) +
  geom_point(
    data = subset(wear_db, !db_is_noise),
    aes(color = db_cluster),
    alpha = 0.80,
    size = 2
  ) +
  labs(
    title = "Wearable data: DBSCAN clusters",
    subtitle = paste0("eps = ", eps_wear, ", minPts = ", minPts_wear, " (noise shown in grey)"),
    x = "Scaled resting heart rate",
    y = "Scaled daily steps",
    color = "DBSCAN cluster"
  ) +
  theme_bw()








The last chunk applies DBSCAN to the wearable dataset after standardizing all physiological variables to ensure that distances are comparable across features. The algorithm is run on the full multivariate feature space (resting heart rate, HRV, steps, skin temperature, oxygen saturation, and sleep efficiency), not just the two variables shown in the final visualization. A k-nearest-neighbor distance plot is first constructed with \(k=\operatorname{minPts}=10\) to guide the choice of \(\varepsilon\). The elbow in this plot suggests a reasonable density threshold, and \(\varepsilon=1.1\) is selected. DBSCAN then assigns each observation either to a densityconnected cluster (positive integer label) or to cluster 0 (noise). The table of cluster counts provides a numerical summary of the partition.
The final figure displays the clustering in a two-dimensional projection (scaled resting heart rate vs. scaled daily steps) for interpretability. Although clustering was performed in the full feature space, this projection reveals several well-separated physiological phenotypes. Points shown in grey correspond to observations that do not belong to any sufficiently dense region under the chosen parameters, while colored points indicate density-connected clusters. In this simulated wearable dataset, DBSCAN identifies distinct groups with coherent physiological profiles while explicitly leaving atypical or isolated patterns unassigned. This illustrates the practical advantage of density-based clustering in healthmonitoring contexts, where unusual or transient states may be better treated as noise rather than forced into predefined clusters.


8.6.4 OPTICS: density structure across scales
A common limitation of DBSCAN is that it assumes a single global density level: one eps value is used everywhere. In real datasets, different clusters may have different densities. For example, one physiological phenotype might be tightly concentrated (high-density cluster), while another is more diffuse (lower-density cluster). A single eps value may either fragment the dense cluster or merge the diffuse cluster with noise.
OPTICS (Ordering Points To Identify the Clustering Structure) addresses this by producing an ordering of points and a reachability distance for each point. Rather than committing to one eps threshold, OPTICS summarizes the density landscape across a range of eps values. The main output is a reachability plot:

Valleys correspond to clusters (high density).
Peaks correspond to transitions between clusters or sparse regions.

Clusters can then be extracted from OPTICS by choosing a reachability threshold or by using automated extraction methods.
Conceptually, OPTICS can be seen as “DBSCAN for multiple eps values,” providing a more robust view when densities vary.
This example applies OPTICS to the same ring dataset previously analyzed with DBSCAN. Unlike DBSCAN, OPTICS does not commit to a single global ε value during clustering. Instead, it computes an ordering of observations together with a reachability distance that reflects the local density structure of the data. The reachability plot displays this structure: valleys correspond to dense, internally connected regions (the rings), while peaks indicate transitions through sparse areas or noise.
Clusters can then be extracted by selecting a reachability threshold (here eps_cl = 0.28), which is conceptually similar to applying DBSCAN at that density level. Because OPTICS captures the density landscape across scales before extraction, it is often more robust when clusters have varying densities or when a single global ε would either fragment a structure or merge distinct regions. In the ring dataset, OPTICS recovers the same non-convex geometry while providing a richer diagnostic view of density structure through the reachability plot.

# ===============================================================
# OPTICS on the same ring dataset used for DBSCAN
# ===============================================================

# Use the same toy_db (two rings + noise)

minPts_opt <- 10

# Fit OPTICS
opt_fit <- dbscan::optics(toy_db[, c("x", "y")],
                          minPts = minPts_opt)

# ---------------------------------------------------------------
# Reachability plot
# ---------------------------------------------------------------
reach_df <- tibble(
  order = seq_along(opt_fit$order),
  reachability = opt_fit$reachdist[opt_fit$order]
) %>%
  mutate(reachability = ifelse(is.finite(reachability),
                               reachability,
                               NA_real_))

p_reach <- ggplot(reach_df, aes(order, reachability)) +
  geom_col(alpha = 0.9) +
  theme_bw() +
  labs(
    title = "OPTICS reachability plot (rings dataset)",
    subtitle = "Valleys correspond to dense ring structures",
    x = "OPTICS ordering",
    y = "Reachability distance"
  )

p_reach







# ---------------------------------------------------------------
# Extract clusters using a chosen reachability threshold
# ---------------------------------------------------------------
eps_extract <- 0.28   # similar scale to DBSCAN example

cl_opt <- dbscan::extractDBSCAN(opt_fit,
                                eps_cl = eps_extract)

toy_opt2 <- toy_db %>%
  mutate(opt_cluster = factor(cl_opt$cluster),
         opt_is_noise = cl_opt$cluster == 0)

ggplot(toy_opt2, aes(x, y)) +
  geom_point(
    data = subset(toy_opt2, opt_is_noise),
    color = "grey60",
    alpha = 0.40,
    size = 1.7
  ) +
  geom_point(
    data = subset(toy_opt2, !opt_is_noise),
    aes(color = opt_cluster),
    alpha = 0.85,
    size = 1.7
  ) +
  coord_equal() +
  theme_bw() +
  labs(
    title = "OPTICS clusters extracted from rings dataset",
    subtitle = paste0("eps_cl = ", eps_extract,
                      ", minPts = ", minPts_opt,
                      " (noise shown in grey)"),
    color = "Cluster"
  )








This figure shows the clusters obtained by applying OPTICS to the two-ring dataset and then extracting clusters using a reachability threshold of \(\varepsilon_{c l}=0.3\) with \(\mathrm{minPts}=10\). The grey points correspond to observations labeled as noise (cluster 0), while colored points indicate density-connected clusters.
Two main features are visible. First, the inner ring is recovered as a single coherent cluster (cluster 1), reflecting its strong and uniform local density. Second, the outer ring is also largely recovered as a connected structure, but it appears split into two clusters (clusters 2 and 3). This split reflects subtle density variations along the ring: although geometrically forming one circular structure, local reachability distances differ slightly across segments, and the chosen extraction threshold separates them into two density-connected components.
Importantly, OPTICS itself does not commit to a fixed global \(\varepsilon\) during ordering. The reachability plot (shown earlier) encodes the density landscape across scales, and clusters are only defined when a specific extraction threshold is applied. Thus, the fragmentation of the outer ring here is not a failure of OPTICS but a consequence of the chosen \(\varepsilon_{c l}\). A slightly larger extraction threshold would likely merge clusters 2 and 3 into a single outer-ring cluster.
Lets now apply optics in our wearables dataset

# ===============================================================
# OPTICS on the wearable dataset (scaled features)
# ===============================================================

# Reuse scaled data from DBSCAN section
# wear_scaled already contains standardized features
# X_wear is the matrix of scaled physiological variables

minPts_opt_wear <- 10

# ---------------------------------------------------------------
# Fit OPTICS
# ---------------------------------------------------------------
opt_wear <- dbscan::optics(X_wear,
                           minPts = minPts_opt_wear)

# ---------------------------------------------------------------
# Reachability plot
# ---------------------------------------------------------------
reach_wear_df <- tibble(
  order = seq_along(opt_wear$order),
  reachability = opt_wear$reachdist[opt_wear$order]
) %>%
  mutate(reachability = ifelse(is.finite(reachability),
                               reachability,
                               NA_real_))

ggplot(reach_wear_df, aes(order, reachability)) +
  geom_col(alpha = 0.9) +
  theme_bw() +
  labs(
    title = "Wearable data: OPTICS reachability plot",
    subtitle = paste0("minPts = ", minPts_opt_wear),
    x = "OPTICS ordering",
    y = "Reachability distance"
  )








The figure above displays the OPTICS reachability plot for the wearable dataset with \(\min \mathrm{Pts}=10\). Each vertical bar represents one observation in the order produced by the OPTICS algorithm, and its height corresponds to the reachability distance-a measure of how far the point must reach to connect to an existing dense region. Low reachability values form visible valleys, which indicate dense and internally coherent regions of the feature space and therefore suggest potential clusters. In contrast, tall peaks correspond to transitions between clusters or to sparse observations that may ultimately be labeled as noise. The presence of multiple broad valleys indicates that the wearable data contain several densitybased subgroups, while differences in valley depth suggest that these groups vary in compactness. Unlike DBSCAN, which requires fixing a single global neighborhood radius in advance, OPTICS first maps the density structure across scales. Clusters are then extracted by choosing a reachability threshold, allowing the analyst to separate stable dense regions while leaving sparse observations unassigned.

# ---------------------------------------------------------------
# Extract clusters using a reachability threshold
# ---------------------------------------------------------------

eps_cl_wear <- 1.1   # Adjust based on reachability plot

cl_wear <- dbscan::extractDBSCAN(opt_wear,
                                 eps_cl = eps_cl_wear)

wear_opt <- wear_scaled %>%
  mutate(
    opt_cluster_num = cl_wear$cluster,
    opt_is_noise    = opt_cluster_num == 0,
    opt_cluster     = factor(opt_cluster_num)
  )

table(wear_opt$opt_cluster)


  0   1   2   3   4 
 16 157 156 155 316 

# ---------------------------------------------------------------
# Visualize in HR vs Steps projection
# ---------------------------------------------------------------
ggplot(wear_opt, aes(HR_mean, steps_mean)) +
  geom_point(
    data = subset(wear_opt, opt_is_noise),
    color = "grey60",
    alpha = 0.45,
    size = 2
  ) +
  geom_point(
    data = subset(wear_opt, !opt_is_noise),
    aes(color = opt_cluster),
    alpha = 0.80,
    size = 2
  ) +
  labs(
    title = "Wearable data: OPTICS clusters",
    subtitle = paste0("eps_cl = ", eps_cl_wear,
                      ", minPts = ", minPts_opt_wear,
                      " (noise shown in grey)"),
    x = "Scaled resting heart rate",
    y = "Scaled daily steps",
    color = "OPTICS cluster"
  ) +
  theme_bw()








The last two example chunks applie OPTICS to the wearable dataset using the same standardized physiological variables previously used for DBSCAN. As with DBSCAN, clustering is performed in the full multivariate feature space rather than only the two variables shown in the visualization. The reachability plot summarizes the density landscape across the dataset: low reachability values (valleys) indicate dense regions, while high values (peaks) correspond to transitions between clusters or sparse observations.
Clusters are then extracted using a reachability threshold \(\varepsilon_{cl}\). Unlike DBSCAN, OPTICS does not rely on a single global neighborhood radius during ordering; instead, it captures density structure across scales before cluster extraction. In the wearable dataset, OPTICS identifies coherent physiological phenotypes while still allowing atypical or weakly connected observations to be labeled as noise. This makes OPTICS particularly useful when cluster densities may vary or when a single fixed \(\varepsilon\) would either fragment dense groups or merge distinct patterns.

section: 8.7 From Hard Clustering to Probabilistic Clustering
text:
8.7 From Hard Clustering to Probabilistic Clustering
Up to this point, clustering has been presented as a geometric partitioning problem. Algorithms such as k-means assign each observation to exactly one cluster by minimizing within-cluster variance. This assignment is deterministic: once the algorithm converges, every observation belongs to a single group with no ambiguity. Such methods are therefore referred to as hard clustering approaches.
However, in many real datasets-particularly in biomedical or physiological contexts-group boundaries are not sharp. Individuals may exhibit intermediate characteristics, partially resembling more than one phenotype. In these settings, it may be more natural to describe cluster membership probabilistically.
Mixture models adopt this perspective. Instead of assuming that clusters are simply regions of space, we assume that the data are generated from a combination of underlying probability distributions. Each cluster corresponds to one component distribution, and each observation has a probability of belonging to each component. This framework is known as probabilistic (or soft) clustering.
Formally, a mixture model assumes that the data distribution can be written as
\[
p(x)=\sum_{k=1}^K \pi_k f_k(x),
\]
where \(\pi_k\) are non-negative mixing proportions that sum to one, and \(f_k(x)\) are component densities. The clustering task becomes the estimation of these components and the probability that each observation was generated by them.

8.7.1 From hard clustering to probabilistic clustering (illustration)
The difference between hard clustering and mixture models becomes clearest when the data are generated by overlapping distributions. In this toy example, observations are drawn from two bivariate Gaussian components whose covariance structures produce elliptical, partially intersecting clouds.
The code makes the generative story explicit in three complementary views. First, a 2D scatterplot shows the sampled points colored by their true generating component, while superimposed contour lines display the true bivariate normal densities for each component. These contours represent level sets of the density function \(f_k(x, y)\), highlighting that separation is not linear and that overlap is expected.
Second, the marginal density plots for \(x\) and \(y\) show the one-dimensional distributions implied by the bivariate model. Even when each variable is considered independently, the components overlap, reinforcing that ambiguity is intrinsic to the data rather than an artifact of the clustering method.
Finally, the 3D surface visualization represents each component density \(f_k(x, y)\) as a landscape over the \((x, y)\) plane. Peaks occur near the component means \(\mu_k\), and the orientation and elongation of the surface reflect the covariance matrices \(\Sigma_k\).
This setup motivates probabilistic clustering: instead of forcing a single label in regions where the component densities overlap, a Gaussian mixture model estimates posterior membership probabilities, \[
P(z_i = k \mid x_i),
\] which quantify how strongly each observation belongs to each component.

# ===============================================================
# Toy data: overlapping Gaussian components
# + marginal normals (x and y)
# + bivariate Gaussian contours (true generating densities)
# + 3D density surfaces (interactive)
# ===============================================================

library(tidyverse)
library(patchwork)
library(mvtnorm)   # dmvnorm for bivariate density
library(plotly)    # 3D surface plots

set.seed(2025)

# ---------------------------------------------------------------
# 1) Parameters: two bivariate Gaussians
# ---------------------------------------------------------------
n <- 450

mu1 <- c(-0.6,  0.2)
mu2 <- c( 0.6, -0.2)

Sigma1 <- matrix(c(1.0,  0.6,
                   0.6,  1.2), 2, 2, byrow = TRUE)

Sigma2 <- matrix(c(1.2, -0.4,
                  -0.4,  0.9), 2, 2, byrow = TRUE)

X1 <- MASS::mvrnorm(n = n, mu = mu1, Sigma = Sigma1)
X2 <- MASS::mvrnorm(n = n, mu = mu2, Sigma = Sigma2)

toy_mix <- bind_rows(
  as_tibble(X1) %>% setNames(c("x","y")) %>% mutate(true = "Component 1"),
  as_tibble(X2) %>% setNames(c("x","y")) %>% mutate(true = "Component 2")
) %>%
  mutate(true = factor(true, levels = c("Component 1","Component 2")))

# ---------------------------------------------------------------
# 2) Consistent palettes (ground-truth components)
# ---------------------------------------------------------------
true_cols <- c(
  "Component 1" = "#E64B35",  # red
  "Component 2" = "#4DBBD5"   # teal
)

# ---------------------------------------------------------------
# 3) Build a grid + evaluate the TRUE bivariate densities
# ---------------------------------------------------------------
pad <- 0.6
x_rng <- range(toy_mix$x) + c(-pad, pad)
y_rng <- range(toy_mix$y) + c(-pad, pad)

x_seq <- seq(x_rng[1], x_rng[2], length.out = 160)
y_seq <- seq(y_rng[1], y_rng[2], length.out = 160)

grid <- expand_grid(x = x_seq, y = y_seq)

grid_dens <- bind_rows(
  grid %>% mutate(true = "Component 1",
                  dens = mvtnorm::dmvnorm(cbind(x,y), mean = mu1, sigma = Sigma1)),
  grid %>% mutate(true = "Component 2",
                  dens = mvtnorm::dmvnorm(cbind(x,y), mean = mu2, sigma = Sigma2))
) %>%
  mutate(true = factor(true, levels = levels(toy_mix$true)))

cont_levels <- grid_dens %>%
  group_by(true) %>%
  summarise(
    l1 = quantile(dens, 0.90),
    l2 = quantile(dens, 0.97),
    l3 = quantile(dens, 0.995),
    .groups = "drop"
  ) %>%
  pivot_longer(cols = starts_with("l"), values_to = "level") %>%
  arrange(true, level) %>%
  distinct(level) %>%
  pull(level)

# ---------------------------------------------------------------
# 4) Plot A: 2D scatter + TRUE bivariate contours
# ---------------------------------------------------------------
p_2d <- ggplot(toy_mix, aes(x, y, color = true)) +
  geom_point(alpha = 0.55, size = 1.6) +
  geom_contour(
    data = grid_dens,
    aes(z = dens, color = true),
    breaks = cont_levels,
    linewidth = 0.9,
    alpha = 0.95
  ) +
  coord_equal() +
  theme_bw() +
  scale_color_manual(values = true_cols) +
  labs(
    title = "Toy data: overlapping Gaussian components",
    subtitle = "Points colored by true generating component; contours show true bivariate normal density",
    color = "True component"
  )

# ---------------------------------------------------------------
# 5) Plot B: marginal distributions (x and y)
# ---------------------------------------------------------------
p_marg_x <- ggplot(toy_mix, aes(x, fill = true)) +
  geom_density(alpha = 0.45, linewidth = 0.9) +
  theme_bw() +
  scale_fill_manual(values = true_cols) +
  labs(
    title = "Marginal distributions: x",
    x = "x", y = "Density", fill = "True component"
  ) +
  theme(legend.position = "none")

p_marg_y <- ggplot(toy_mix, aes(y, fill = true)) +
  geom_density(alpha = 0.45, linewidth = 0.9) +
  theme_bw() +
  scale_fill_manual(values = true_cols) +
  labs(
    title = "Marginal distributions: y",
    x = "y", y = "Density", fill = "True component"
  ) +
  theme(legend.position = "none")

# ---------------------------------------------------------------
# 6) Plot C: 3D density surfaces (interactive)
# ---------------------------------------------------------------
# Helper: convert grid densities into matrices for plotly surface()
dens_to_mat <- function(df, x_vals, y_vals) {
  df %>%
    arrange(y, x) %>%
    pull(dens) %>%
    matrix(nrow = length(y_vals), ncol = length(x_vals), byrow = TRUE)
}

z1 <- dens_to_mat(filter(grid_dens, true == "Component 1"), x_seq, y_seq)
z2 <- dens_to_mat(filter(grid_dens, true == "Component 2"), x_seq, y_seq)

# One surface per component (separate)
p_3d_c1 <- plot_ly(x = x_seq, y = y_seq, z = z1, type = "surface", opacity = 0.95) %>%
  layout(
    title = "3D density surface: Component 1",
    scene = list(
      xaxis = list(title = "x"),
      yaxis = list(title = "y"),
      zaxis = list(title = "Density")
    )
  )

p_3d_c2 <- plot_ly(x = x_seq, y = y_seq, z = z2, type = "surface", opacity = 0.95) %>%
  layout(
    title = "3D density surface: Component 2",
    scene = list(
      xaxis = list(title = "x"),
      yaxis = list(title = "y"),
      zaxis = list(title = "Density")
    )
  )

# Overlay (both surfaces together)
p_3d_overlay <- plot_ly() %>%
  add_surface(x = x_seq, y = y_seq, z = z1, opacity = 0.70, name = "Component 1") %>%
  add_surface(x = x_seq, y = y_seq, z = z2, opacity = 0.70, name = "Component 2") %>%
  layout(
    title = "3D density surfaces (overlay)",
    scene = list(
      xaxis = list(title = "x"),
      yaxis = list(title = "y"),
      zaxis = list(title = "Density")
    )
  )

# ---------------------------------------------------------------
# 7) Outputs (as you requested: one per row)
# ---------------------------------------------------------------
p_2d







p_marg_x







p_marg_y







# 3D (pick ONE or show all; overlay is usually enough)
p_3d_overlay




# p_3d_c1
# p_3d_c2


8.7.1.1 Hard clustering: k-means forces a single label
k-means produces a deterministic partition: every point is assigned to exactly one cluster. In overlapping regions, this creates an artificial “hard boundary”, because the algorithm has no mechanism to express uncertainty. This is often fine for clean, well-separated, spherical groups, but it can be limiting when phenotypes overlap or when measurements are noisy.

# ===============================================================
# Hard clustering: k-means (k = 2)
# ===============================================================

# ===============================================================
# Hard clustering: k-means (k = 2)
# ===============================================================

set.seed(2025)

km <- kmeans(toy_mix[, c("x","y")], centers = 2, nstart = 30)

toy_km <- toy_mix %>%
  mutate(km_cluster = factor(km$cluster))

# New color palette for k-means (distinct from true colors)
km_cols <- c(
  "1" = "#3C5488",   # dark blue
  "2" = "#F39B7F"    # soft orange
)

p_km <- ggplot(toy_km, aes(x, y, color = km_cluster)) +
  geom_point(alpha = 0.70, size = 1.6) +
  coord_equal() +
  theme_bw() +
  scale_color_manual(values = km_cols) +
  labs(
    title = "k-means (hard assignments)",
    subtitle = "Algorithmic partition (forced boundary in overlap)",
    color = "k-means cluster"
  )

p_raw 







p_km








The first figure shows the true generating components used to simulate the data, colored according to their underlying Gaussian source. Although two distinct distributions were used, the overlap region reveals that membership is not visually separable by a sharp boundary. The second figure in the last sequence displays the k-means partition of the same dataset. Importantly, the color scheme differs from the true source to emphasize that k-means is recovering clusters based solely on geometric proximity, not on knowledge of the data-generating mechanism. In the central overlap region, points that visually belong to both generating components are nonetheless assigned deterministically to a single cluster. This illustrates the defining characteristic of hard clustering: every observation must belong to exactly one group, even when the underlying structure is ambiguous.



8.7.2 Gaussian Mixture Models (GMM)
The most widely used mixture model for continuous data is the Gaussian Mixture Model (GMM). In this case, each component \(f_k(x)\) is assumed to be a multivariate normal distribution:
\[
f_k(x)=\mathcal{N}\left(x \mid \mu_k, \Sigma_k\right) .
\]
Each cluster is therefore characterized by:

A mean vector \(\mu_k\) (its center),
A covariance matrix \(\Sigma_k\) (its shape and orientation),
A mixing proportion \(\pi_k\) (its relative size).

This formulation is substantially more flexible than k -means. Because covariance matrices are estimated for each component, clusters may be:

Spherical or elongated,
Axis-aligned or rotated,
Compact or diffuse.

The next figure represents these clusters structures. We generate three components with different shapes and characteristics and then check if GMM can guess the right cluster structures.

# ===============================================================
# Contrast palettes: simulated truth vs clustering output
# ===============================================================

library(tidyverse)
library(MASS)
library(mclust)
library(patchwork)

set.seed(2025)

# ---- helper: rotated covariance ----
rot_cov <- function(a, b, angle_rad) {
  R <- matrix(c(cos(angle_rad), -sin(angle_rad),
                sin(angle_rad),  cos(angle_rad)), nrow = 2, byrow = TRUE)
  D <- diag(c(a, b))
  R %*% D %*% t(R)
}

n <- 250

# 1) Spherical + compact
mu1 <- c(-3,  2)
S1  <- diag(c(0.25, 0.25))

# 2) Axis-aligned elongated (diffuse along x)
mu2 <- c( 0,  0)
S2  <- diag(c(1.8, 0.25))

# 3) Rotated elongated
mu3 <- c( 3,  2)
S3  <- rot_cov(a = 1.6, b = 0.25, angle_rad = pi/4)

X1 <- MASS::mvrnorm(n, mu = mu1, Sigma = S1)
X2 <- MASS::mvrnorm(n, mu = mu2, Sigma = S2)
X3 <- MASS::mvrnorm(n, mu = mu3, Sigma = S3)

toy_gmm <- bind_rows(
  as_tibble(X1) %>% setNames(c("x","y")) %>% mutate(true = "Component 1"),
  as_tibble(X2) %>% setNames(c("x","y")) %>% mutate(true = "Component 2"),
  as_tibble(X3) %>% setNames(c("x","y")) %>% mutate(true = "Component 3")
)

# ---------------------------------------------------------------
# Palette A (SIMULATED truth): choose a manual palette you like
# (These are vibrant and distinct, but you can swap as you wish.)
# ---------------------------------------------------------------
true_cols <- c(
  "Component 1" = "#1B9E77",  # teal
  "Component 2" = "#D95F02",  # orange
  "Component 3" = "#7570B3"   # purple
)

p_true <- ggplot(toy_gmm, aes(x, y, color = true)) +
  geom_point(alpha = 0.65, size = 1.6) +
  coord_equal() +
  theme_bw() +
  scale_color_manual(values = true_cols) +
  labs(
    title = "Toy data: simulated components (ground truth)",
    subtitle = "Colors reflect the data-generating component",
    color = "True component"
  )

# ---------------------------------------------------------------
# Fit a GMM (soft clustering model; here we plot hard labels from MAP)
# ---------------------------------------------------------------
fit <- Mclust(toy_gmm[, c("x","y")], G = 3)
toy_fit <- toy_gmm %>%
  mutate(gmm_cluster = factor(fit$classification))

# ---------------------------------------------------------------
# Palette B (CLUSTER output): a *different* palette family
# Brewer palettes are great for contrast with manual colors above.
# Options: "Set1", "Set2", "Dark2"
# ---------------------------------------------------------------
cluster_palette <- "Set1"

p_gmm <- ggplot(toy_fit, aes(x, y, color = gmm_cluster)) +
  geom_point(alpha = 0.70, size = 1.6) +
  coord_equal() +
  theme_bw() +
  scale_color_brewer(palette = cluster_palette) +
  labs(
    title = "GMM clustering result (estimated labels)",
    subtitle = paste0("Model: ", fit$modelName, " | G = ", fit$G),
    color = "GMM cluster"
  )

p_true 







p_gmm








The upper panel displays the simulated data-generating structure: three Gaussian components with distinct covariance patterns. One component is compact and approximately spherical, another is more diffuse and elongated along a horizontal axis, and the third is elongated and rotated, producing a tilted elliptical shape. These colors represent the true underlying distributions used to generate the data and therefore serve as ground truth. The lower panel shows the clustering result obtained from a Gaussian Mixture Model (GMM), where labels are estimated from the fitted model rather than known a priori. Despite not having access to the true component labels, the GMM successfully recovers the three distinct groups and their differing geometric structures. The selected model (“VVV”) indicates that each component is allowed its own covariance matrix, enabling the algorithm to capture differences in shape, orientation, and dispersion.
Most importantly, cluster membership is soft. For each observation \(x_i\), the model estimates posterior probabilities:
\[
P\left(z_i=k \mid x_i\right),
\]
which represent the probability that observation \(i\) belongs to cluster \(k\). Final cluster labels may be obtained by selecting the maximum probability, but the full probabilistic information is retained.
This probabilistic framework is particularly appealing when groups overlap or when uncertainty is scientifically meaningful. The following code allow us to extract such probabilities.

# ===============================================================
# Fit GMM on toy_mix and extract posterior probabilities (aligned)
# ===============================================================

# 1) Fit the GMM on the SAME data you will bind to
fit <- Mclust(toy_mix[, c("x","y")], G = 2)

# 2) Posterior membership probabilities: N x G
post_probs <- as_tibble(fit$z)
colnames(post_probs) <- paste0("P(Component_", seq_len(ncol(post_probs)), ")")

# 3) Build a single tibble (same number of rows guaranteed)
toy_probs <- toy_mix %>%
  bind_cols(post_probs) %>%
  mutate(
    MAP_cluster = factor(fit$classification),   # most likely component
    max_prob    = apply(fit$z, 1, max),
    uncertainty = 1 - max_prob
  ) %>%
  dplyr::select(
    x, y, true,
    dplyr::starts_with("P("),
    MAP_cluster, max_prob, uncertainty
  )

# quick check
stopifnot(nrow(toy_probs) == nrow(toy_mix))

toy_probs %>% dplyr::slice_head(n = 12)

# A tibble: 12 × 8
         x       y true   `P(Component_1)` `P(Component_2)` MAP_cluster max_prob

12 -1.85   -1.75   Compo…          0.00314            0.997 2              0.997
# ℹ 1 more variable: uncertainty <dbl>


In the last table, the two columns \(\mathrm{P}(\) Component_1) and \(\mathrm{P}(\) Component_2 \()\) are the posterior membership probabilities from the fitted Gaussian mixture model: for each observation (each row), they quantify how likely it is that the point was generated by each Gaussian component, and they always sum to 1 . The column MAP_cluster is the hard label induced by the soft model (Maximum A Posteriori assignment): it simply picks the component with the larger posterior probability for that point, so it’s the “most likely” cluster under the mixture model. The quantity max_prob \(=\max (\mathrm{P}(\) Component_1), P (Component_2) ) measures how confident the model is about that MAP label: values near 1 indicate the point sits in a region clearly dominated by one component, while values near 0.5 indicate the point lies in the overlap where both components explain it almost equally well. Finally, uncertainty = 1 - max_prob is a convenient uncertainty score: it is close to 0 for unambiguous points (e.g., max_prob \(\approx 0.95 \rightarrow\) uncertainty \(\approx\) 0.05 ) and it approaches 0.5 when membership is highly ambiguous (max_prob \(\approx 0.50 \rightarrow\) uncertainty \(\approx 0.50\) ). This is exactly the “soft clustering” benefit: you keep both a crisp label (MAP_cluster ) and a numeric measure of ambiguity ( uncertainty) that is scientifically meaningful when groups overlap.

8.7.2.1 Most ambiguous observations (highest uncertainty).
We can use the following code to check the overlaps:

toy_probs %>%
  arrange(desc(uncertainty)) %>%
  slice_head(n = 12)

The last table lists the observations with the largest uncertainty values, obtained by sorting in descending order of \(1-\max _k P\left(z_i=k \mid x_i\right)\). These points exhibit posterior probabilities very close to 0.5 for both components (e.g., 0.501 vs 0.499 ), indicating that the model assigns nearly equal likelihood to each cluster. Such observations lie in the geometric overlap between the two Gaussian components and therefore represent genuinely ambiguous cases. This output illustrates the core advantage of probabilistic clustering: instead of forcing a sharp boundary, the model explicitly quantifies uncertainty for points that cannot be confidently assigned to a single group.
We can use the following code to visualise the ambiguous points.

# ===============================================================
# Cleaner plot: clusters (color) + ambiguous points highlighted
# - Typical points: small + transparent
# - Ambiguous points: larger, black outline, plotted on top
# ===============================================================

library(tidyverse)

p_top <- 0.05
thr <- quantile(toy_probs$uncertainty, probs = 1 - p_top, na.rm = TRUE)

toy_plot <- toy_probs %>%
  mutate(ambiguous = uncertainty >= thr)

ggplot() +
  # typical points (background)
  geom_point(
    data = subset(toy_plot, !ambiguous),
    aes(x, y, color = MAP_cluster),
    alpha = 0.35,
    size  = 1.6
  ) +
  # ambiguous points (foreground)
  geom_point(
    data = subset(toy_plot, ambiguous),
    aes(x, y, color = MAP_cluster),
    shape = 21,          # filled circle with outline
    fill  = "white",
    stroke = 1.1,
    size  = 3.0,
    alpha = 1.0
  ) +
  coord_equal() +
  theme_bw() +
  labs(
    title = "GMM clustering with uncertainty highlighted",
    subtitle = paste0(
      "Color = MAP cluster; highlighted points are the most ambiguous (top ",
      round(100*p_top), "% by uncertainty)"
    ),
    color = "MAP cluster"
  ) +
  theme(
    legend.position = "right"
  )










8.7.2.2 Cluster-level summary of certainty.
The following code provide us with cluster summaries

toy_probs %>%
  group_by(MAP_cluster) %>%
  summarise(
    n = n(),
    mean_max_prob = mean(max_prob),
    mean_uncertainty = mean(uncertainty),
    .groups = "drop"
  )

# A tibble: 2 × 4
  MAP_cluster     n mean_max_prob mean_uncertainty
  <fct>       <int>         <dbl>            <dbl>
1 1             360         0.798            0.202
2 2             540         0.733            0.267


The second table summarizes classification confidence at the cluster level. For each MAP cluster, it reports the number of assigned observations, the average maximum posterior probability, and the average uncertainty. Cluster 1 shows a higher mean maximum probability (≈ 0.80) and lower mean uncertainty (≈ 0.20), indicating more clearly separated observations. Cluster 2 has a lower mean maximum probability (≈ 0.73) and higher mean uncertainty (≈ 0.27), suggesting greater overlap with the other component. This aggregate view provides a quantitative assessment of how well-separated the clusters are, complementing the visual inspection of overlap in the scatter plot.



8.7.3 The EM Algorithm (Conceptual Overview)
Estimating a Gaussian mixture model requires determining the unknown parameters \(\left\{\pi_k, \mu_k, \Sigma_k\right\}_{k=1}^K\). Direct maximization of the likelihood is challenging because cluster memberships are latent (unobserved). The standard solution is the Expectation-Maximization (EM) algorithm.
The EM algorithm proceeds iteratively in two alternating steps:
E-step (Expectation step). Given current parameter estimates, compute the posterior probability that each observation belongs to each cluster. These probabilities act as soft assignments.
M-step (Maximization step). Update the parameters \(\pi_k, \mu_k, \Sigma_k\) by maximizing the expected complete-data likelihood, using the probabilities computed in the E-step as weights.
These two steps are repeated until convergence. Intuitively, the algorithm alternates between estimating cluster memberships (softly) and updating cluster parameters, gradually refining both.
Unlike k-means, which minimizes a geometric criterion, EM maximizes a probabilistic likelihood function.


8.7.4 Comparison with k-means
Gaussian mixture models generalize k-means. In fact, k-means can be viewed as a special limiting case of a GMM under restrictive assumptions:

All clusters share identical covariance matrices

Covariance matrices are spherical (proportional to the identity matrix)

Variance tends toward zero

Hard assignments are used instead of probabilities

Under these assumptions, maximizing the Gaussian mixture likelihood becomes equivalent to minimizing within-cluster sum of squares, which is precisely the k-means objective.
The key differences can be summarized as follows:








Feature
k-means
GMM




Assignment
Hard
Soft (probabilistic)


Cluster shape
Spherical
Elliptical (flexible covariance)


Objective
Minimize WCSS
Maximize likelihood


Uncertainty
Not available
Explicit posterior probabilities





8.7.5 Fitting GMM into the wearables example

# ===============================================================
# GMM clustering (Gaussian Mixture Models) on the wearable dataset
# - Fits a multivariate Gaussian mixture on the SCALED feature matrix
# - Returns: MAP cluster labels + posterior probabilities + uncertainty
# - Visualizes in a familiar 2D plane (HR_mean vs steps_mean)
# ===============================================================

# ---------------------------------------------------------------
# 1) Load + scale features (same convention as k-means/DBSCAN)
# ---------------------------------------------------------------
wear <- readRDS("~/att_ai_ml/att_book/data/wearable_cluster.rds")

feat_cols <- c("HR_mean","HRV_sdnn","steps_mean","skin_temp","spo2","sleep_eff")

wear_scaled <- wear %>%
  mutate(across(all_of(feat_cols), ~ as.numeric(scale(.))))

X_wear <- wear_scaled %>% dplyr::select(all_of(feat_cols)) %>% as.matrix()

# ---------------------------------------------------------------
# 2) Fit a GMM
# Option A (recommended for teaching): choose G explicitly
# ---------------------------------------------------------------
G <- 4  # set to your preferred number of clusters/components
fit_gmm <- Mclust(X_wear, G = G)

# (Optional) Option B: let mclust choose G via BIC
# fit_gmm <- Mclust(X_wear)  # auto-selects G and covariance model

# Inspect chosen model
fit_gmm$modelName

[1] "VVV"

fit_gmm$G

[1] 4

# ---------------------------------------------------------------
# 3) Posterior probabilities + MAP labels + uncertainty
# ---------------------------------------------------------------
post_probs <- as_tibble(fit_gmm$z)
colnames(post_probs) <- paste0("P(Component_", seq_len(ncol(post_probs)), ")")

wear_gmm <- wear_scaled %>%
  bind_cols(post_probs) %>%
  mutate(
    MAP_cluster = factor(fit_gmm$classification),
    max_prob    = apply(fit_gmm$z, 1, max),
    uncertainty = 1 - max_prob
  )

# Quick summaries
table(wear_gmm$MAP_cluster)


  1   2   3   4 
160 320 160 160 

wear_gmm %>%
  group_by(MAP_cluster) %>%
  summarise(
    n = n(),
    mean_max_prob = mean(max_prob),
    mean_uncertainty = mean(uncertainty),
    .groups = "drop"
  )

# A tibble: 4 × 4
  MAP_cluster     n mean_max_prob mean_uncertainty
  <fct>       <int>         <dbl>            <dbl>
1 1             160         1             0       
2 2             320         1             0       
3 3             160         1.000         9.04e-10
4 4             160         1             0       

# ---------------------------------------------------------------
# 4) Plot: clusters in 2D (projection only)
# ---------------------------------------------------------------
ggplot(wear_gmm, aes(HR_mean, steps_mean, color = MAP_cluster)) +
  geom_point(alpha = 0.80, size = 2) +
  labs(
    title = "Wearable data: GMM clusters (MAP labels)",
    subtitle = paste0(
      "Fitted on all scaled features (", paste(feat_cols, collapse = ", "),
      "); shown here in HR_mean vs steps_mean projection\n",
      "Model: ", fit_gmm$modelName, " | G = ", fit_gmm$G
    ),
    x = "Scaled resting heart rate",
    y = "Scaled daily steps",
    color = "GMM (MAP) cluster"
  ) +
  theme_bw()







# ---------------------------------------------------------------
# 5) (Optional) Flag most ambiguous points (top 5% uncertainty)
# ---------------------------------------------------------------
thr <- quantile(wear_gmm$uncertainty, 0.95, na.rm = TRUE)

wear_gmm <- wear_gmm %>%
  mutate(ambiguous = ifelse(uncertainty >= thr, "Ambiguous (top 5%)", "Typical"))

ggplot(wear_gmm, aes(HR_mean, steps_mean)) +
  geom_point(
    data = subset(wear_gmm, ambiguous == "Typical"),
    aes(color = MAP_cluster),
    alpha = 0.70, size = 2
  ) +
  geom_point(
    data = subset(wear_gmm, ambiguous != "Typical"),
    aes(color = MAP_cluster, shape = ambiguous),
    alpha = 0.95, size = 2.6, stroke = 0.9
  ) +
  labs(
    title = "Wearable data: GMM clustering with ambiguity flagged",
    subtitle = paste0("Color = MAP cluster; shape flags highest-uncertainty points (top 5%). Model: ",
                      fit_gmm$modelName, " | G = ", fit_gmm$G),
    x = "Scaled resting heart rate",
    y = "Scaled daily steps",
    color = "MAP cluster",
    shape = NULL
  ) +
  theme_bw()
