title: 8  Clustering
text:
8.8 Hierarchical Clustering
Hierarchical clustering provides a flexible framework for uncovering structure in multivariate datasets without committing to a fixed number of clusters in advance. Rather than producing a single partition, the method constructs a hierarchy of nested groupings, represented visually by a dendrogram. This tree-like structure reveals how similarity relationships evolve as increasingly dissimilar observations are merged together.
In the present example, each observation corresponds to a patient and each feature corresponds to a gene. The expression matrix is therefore organised as patients × genes, meaning that clustering operates across rows. The objective is to determine whether patients with similar molecular activation patterns naturally group together and whether the resulting hierarchy reflects the simulated biological subtypes embedded in the data generation process.

library(tidyverse)
library(pheatmap)

expr_matrix <- readRDS("~/att_ai_ml/att_book/data/simulated_genomic_matrix.rds")
group       <- readRDS("~/att_ai_ml/att_book/data/simulated_genomic_groups.rds")

# Annotation to compare clustering vs. known subtype
ann <- tibble(Group = group) |> as.data.frame()
rownames(ann) <- rownames(expr_matrix)

dim(expr_matrix)

[1]  60 300

table(group)

group
   A_IFN B_Inflam  C_Metab 
      20       20       20 


The dataset consists of 60 patients measured across 300 genes. The group vector encodes the simulated biological subtype for each patient, which we will later use as a reference to evaluate whether the clustering procedure recovers the underlying structure embedded during data generation.
The three groups displayed above correspond to the simulated biological subtypes embedded in the data generation process. Each patient was assigned to one of three latent molecular programs: an interferon-dominant profile (A_IFN), an inflammation-dominant profile (B_Inflam), or a metabolic-dominant profile (C_Metab). These labels represent the underlying ground truth structure intentionally introduced during simulation. They are not derived from clustering; rather, they provide a reference against which clustering performance can later be evaluated. By comparing the hierarchical clustering solution to these known subtype assignments, we can assess whether the algorithm successfully recovers the biological structure that was embedded in the expression matrix.
This perspective aligns directly with clinical applications of clustering in omics research. When patients are clustered based on gene expression, the goal is typically to uncover molecular subtypes, identify latent biological programs, or reveal stratification relevant for prognosis or treatment response.

8.8.1 Intuition: how a dendrogram is constructed
To build intuition, imagine a small set of observations placed in a two-dimensional feature space. Some observations are very close to each other, while others are clearly separated. Hierarchical clustering begins with every observation as its own cluster. It then repeatedly merges the two clusters that are most similar under the chosen distance measure.
The dendrogram is simply a visual record of these merge operations. Each horizontal connection represents a merge event. The vertical axis (the height of the merge) corresponds to the dissimilarity between the two clusters at the moment they were fused.
If two observations merge at a very low height, they are highly similar. If two larger clusters merge only at a high height, this indicates that they were relatively dissimilar, and the algorithm had to tolerate a greater degree of heterogeneity to combine them.
In this way, a dendrogram encodes multi-scale structure: early merges reveal tight local similarity, while later merges reveal broader groupings.

req <- c("tibble", "dplyr", "ggplot2", "patchwork", "png", "grid")
to_install <- setdiff(req, rownames(installed.packages()))
if (length(to_install) > 0) install.packages(to_install)

library(tibble)
library(dplyr)
library(ggplot2)
library(patchwork)

# ------------------------------------------------------------
# 1) Toy points with more spacing (keeps merge logic: A~C, then +B; D~E)
# ------------------------------------------------------------
pts <- tibble(
  id = c("A","B","C","D","E"),
  x  = c(-0.45, 0.55, -0.25, 3.10, 3.55),
  y  = c( 0.55, 0.80,  0.15, 2.55, 2.05)
)

# ------------------------------------------------------------
# 2) Ellipse helper
# ------------------------------------------------------------
make_ellipse <- function(df, n = 240, scale = 2.2, min_minor = 0.10) {
  stopifnot(nrow(df) >= 2)
  x <- df$x; y <- df$y
  mu <- c(mean(x), mean(y))

  if (nrow(df) >= 3) {
    S <- stats::cov(cbind(x, y))
    eig <- eigen(S, symmetric = TRUE)
    vals <- pmax(eig$values, 1e-8)
    R <- eig$vectors

    t <- seq(0, 2*pi, length.out = n)
    circle <- rbind(cos(t), sin(t))
    radii <- scale * sqrt(vals)
    ell <- t(R %*% diag(radii) %*% circle)
    return(tibble(x = mu[1] + ell[,1], y = mu[2] + ell[,2]))
  }

  # nrow == 2: ellipse around segment
  v <- c(x[2] - x[1], y[2] - y[1])
  L <- sqrt(sum(v^2))
  if (L < 1e-8) L <- 1e-8

  angle <- atan2(v[2], v[1])
  major <- (L/2) * scale
  minor <- max(min_minor, (L/2) * 0.35)

  t <- seq(0, 2*pi, length.out = n)
  ex <- major * cos(t)
  ey <- minor * sin(t)

  xr <- ex * cos(angle) - ey * sin(angle)
  yr <- ex * sin(angle) + ey * cos(angle)

  tibble(x = mu[1] + xr, y = mu[2] + yr)
}

ell_ac  <- make_ellipse(filter(pts, id %in% c("A","C"))) |> mutate(tag = "AC")
ell_abc <- make_ellipse(filter(pts, id %in% c("A","B","C"))) |> mutate(tag = "ABC")
ell_de  <- make_ellipse(filter(pts, id %in% c("D","E"))) |> mutate(tag = "DE")
ell_all <- make_ellipse(pts, scale = 2.35) |> mutate(tag = "ALL")
# ------------------------------------------------------------
# 3) Feature space plot (better colors + spacing + nicer theme)
# ------------------------------------------------------------
p_space <- ggplot(pts, aes(x, y)) +

  # Big dashed ellipse (ALL)
  geom_path(data = ell_all,
            aes(x, y),
            inherit.aes = FALSE,
            linewidth = 1.1,
            linetype = "22",
            colour = "#222222") +

  # ABC ellipse (red)
  geom_path(data = ell_abc,
            aes(x, y),
            inherit.aes = FALSE,
            linewidth = 1.2,
            colour = "#D55E00") +

  # DE ellipse (green)
  geom_path(data = ell_de,
            aes(x, y),
            inherit.aes = FALSE,
            linewidth = 1.2,
            colour = "#009E73") +

  geom_point(size = 4, colour = "#111111") +
  geom_text(aes(label = id), nudge_y = 0.18, size = 5) +
  labs(
    title = "Observations in feature space",
    x = "Feature 1",
    y = "Feature 2"
  ) +
  scale_x_continuous(expand = expansion(mult = c(0.10, 0.10))) +
  scale_y_continuous(expand = expansion(mult = c(0.12, 0.10))) +
  theme_minimal(base_size = 14) +
  theme(
    panel.grid.minor = element_blank(),
    plot.title = element_text(face = "bold"),
    axis.title = element_text(face = "bold")
  )
# ------------------------------------------------------------
# 4) Dendrogram from the same points (base plot -> PNG -> panel)
# ------------------------------------------------------------
dist_pts <- dist(as.matrix(dplyr::select(pts, x, y)), method = "euclidean")
hc <- hclust(dist_pts, method = "complete")

tmp <- tempfile(fileext = ".png")
png(tmp, width = 950, height = 900, res = 160)
par(mar = c(5, 4, 4, 1))
plot(hc,
     main = "Dendrogram",
     xlab = "",
     sub = "",
     ylab = "Height (merge distance)",
     labels = pts$id)
dev.off()

quartz_off_screen 
                2 

p_dend <- ggplot() +
  annotation_custom(grid::rasterGrob(png::readPNG(tmp), interpolate = TRUE),
                    xmin = -Inf, xmax = Inf, ymin = -Inf, ymax = Inf) +
  theme_void()

# ------------------------------------------------------------
# 5) Combine panels
# ------------------------------------------------------------
(p_space | p_dend) + plot_layout(widths = c(1.2, 1))








The left panel shows how geometric proximity in feature space gives rise to nested groupings. The right panel shows the corresponding dendrogram built from the same points. The merge heights on the vertical axis reflect the distances between clusters at the time they were joined, translating spatial separation into hierarchical structure.


8.8.2 Agglomerative cluster
In agglomerative hierarchical clustering, each patient begins as its own cluster. At each iteration, the two most similar clusters are merged. This process continues until all patients are joined into a single cluster. The full sequence of merges defines the dendrogram.
Two modelling decisions govern this process. The first is the choice of dissimilarity measure between patients. Because gene expression values may vary in scale, it is standard practice to standardize features before computing distances. When Euclidean distance is used after standardization, differences reflect overall molecular pattern similarity rather than absolute magnitude differences.
The second decision concerns the linkage criterion, which defines how distances between clusters are computed once clusters contain more than one patient. Different linkage rules encode different notions of what a “coherent” cluster should look like. For example, single linkage uses the minimum pairwise distance between members of two clusters, complete linkage uses the maximum, average linkage uses the mean, and Ward’s method merges the pair of clusters that produces the smallest increase in within-cluster variance. In high-dimensional biomedical data, Ward’s method is often a sensible default because it tends to yield compact, relatively homogeneous patient groups.

# Standardize genes (columns): patients x genes
expr_scaled <- scale(expr_matrix)

# Euclidean distance between patients (rows)
dist_mat <- dist(expr_scaled, method = "euclidean")

as.matrix(dist_mat)[1:6, 1:6]

         Patient1 Patient2 Patient3 Patient4 Patient5 Patient6
Patient1  0.00000 14.26630 14.00825 14.82618 13.74518 13.42611
Patient2 14.26630  0.00000 12.44615 12.54622 12.13723 13.51659
Patient3 14.00825 12.44615  0.00000 13.55047 12.79358 12.59888
Patient4 14.82618 12.54622 13.55047  0.00000 12.02568 13.57530
Patient5 13.74518 12.13723 12.79358 12.02568  0.00000 12.60601
Patient6 13.42611 13.51659 12.59888 13.57530 12.60601  0.00000


The distance matrix encodes pairwise Euclidean distances between patients after gene standardization. Each entry represents how dissimilar two patients are across the entire gene panel. This matrix serves as the input to the hierarchical clustering algorithm.
In gene-expression analysis, the choice of dissimilarity measure is not purely technical. While Euclidean distance on standardized data captures overall magnitude differences across genes, many omics applications prioritize similarity in expression patterns rather than absolute levels. In such cases, correlation-based dissimilarities are often more appropriate, as they measure co-variation across genes.
Correlation distance is typically defined as \[d_{ij} = 1 - \rho_{ij},\] , where \(rho\) is the Pearson correlation between two patient expression profiles.

# Correlation-based distance between patients
cor_mat <- cor(t(expr_scaled), method = "pearson")
dist_cor <- as.dist(1 - cor_mat)

hc_cor <- hclust(dist_cor, method = "average")

plot(hc_cor, labels = FALSE,
     main = "Hierarchical clustering — correlation distance",
     xlab = "Patients", sub = "")










8.8.3 Divisive hierarchical clustering
Agglomerative methods construct the hierarchy by progressively merging the closest clusters. Divisive methods follow the opposite logic: they begin with all observations grouped together and recursively split clusters into increasingly smaller components.
Conceptually, divisive clustering can be appealing in biomedical contexts because it often isolates the dominant axis of variation first. For example, if one molecular subtype differs strongly from the others, a divisive method may separate it at the top of the hierarchy before exploring finer subdivisions within each branch.
Although less commonly used in large-scale omics due to computational cost, divisive approaches provide an important conceptual complement to agglomerative methods. They reinforce the idea that a dendrogram represents multi-scale structure, independent of whether it is constructed through merging or splitting.

if (!requireNamespace("cluster", quietly = TRUE)) install.packages("cluster")
library(cluster)

# Fit divisive hierarchical clustering (DIANA)
diana_fit <- diana(dist_mat)

# Plot dendrogram
plot(diana_fit, main = "Divisive clustering (DIANA)", labels = FALSE)














# Cut at k = 3 for comparison
cluster_diana_k3 <- cutree(as.hclust(diana_fit), k = 3)

table(True = group, Cluster = cluster_diana_k3)

          Cluster
True        1  2  3
  A_IFN    20  0  0
  B_Inflam  0 20  0
  C_Metab   1  0 19


The contingency table allows us to compare divisive clustering with the known subtype labels. Differences relative to the agglomerative Ward solution illustrate how algorithmic assumptions influence hierarchical structure. While both methods produce dendrograms, the sequence of splits and merges can emphasize different aspects of the data.


8.8.4 Building the model
The construction of the hierarchical model follows a clear sequence. First, the gene expression matrix is standardized across columns so that each gene contributes comparably to patient dissimilarity. Next, a pairwise distance matrix between patients is computed. Finally, the hierarchical clustering algorithm is applied using the chosen linkage method.

hc_patients <- hclust(dist_mat, method = "ward.D2")

plot(hc_patients, labels = FALSE,
     main = "Hierarchical clustering (patients) — Ward.D2",
     xlab = "Patients", sub = "")








The resulting object encodes the full merge history. Converting it into a dendrogram allows us to visualize how patients cluster together across multiple similarity thresholds. Patients that merge at low heights share highly similar molecular profiles, whereas merges at larger heights reflect more substantial differences.
At this stage, no decision about the number of clusters has yet been imposed. The dendrogram contains information at all possible resolutions.


8.8.5 Cutting the trees
Although hierarchical clustering does not require specifying the number of clusters in advance, practical analysis often involves selecting a flat partition by cutting the dendrogram at a chosen height. In this example, we cut the tree at \(k=3\), reflecting the three simulated biological subtypes used to generate the data.

k <- 3
cluster_k3 <- cutree(hc_patients, k = k)

# Visual: highlight clusters on dendrogram
plot(hc_patients, labels = FALSE, main = "Cut at k = 3")
rect.hclust(hc_patients, k = k, border = 2:6)







# Compare with known truth (group)
tab <- table(True = group, Cluster = cluster_k3)
tab

          Cluster
True        1  2  3
  A_IFN    20  0  0
  B_Inflam  0 20  0
  C_Metab   0  0 20


The resulting partition assigns each patient to one of three clusters. Comparing these assignments with the known subtype labels stored in group allows us to evaluate whether hierarchical clustering successfully recovers the underlying biological structure.

# Adjusted Rand Index (agreement between clustering and true groups)
if (!requireNamespace("mclust", quietly = TRUE)) install.packages("mclust")
ari <- mclust::adjustedRandIndex(as.integer(factor(group)), cluster_k3)
ari

[1] 1


When the dendrogram separation aligns with the simulated subtypes, it demonstrates that the clustering procedure is capturing meaningful molecular similarity rather than random variation.


8.8.6 Choosing the number of clusters
Selecting the number of clusters from a dendrogram is inherently interpretative. Visual inspection of merge heights can reveal natural separation scales: large vertical gaps between successive merges often indicate potential boundaries between clusters.
To complement visual inspection, internal validation metrics can be computed across a range of candidate values of \(k\). Indices such as the Davies-Bouldin index or Dunn index provide quantitative summaries of cluster compactness and separation. In practice, one often examines these metrics for \(k=2,3,4, \ldots\) and looks for stable or optimal regions rather than a single sharp optimum.

if (!requireNamespace("cluster", quietly = TRUE)) install.packages("cluster")
library(cluster)

k_grid <- 2:8

sil_mean <- map_dbl(k_grid, function(kk) {
  cl <- cutree(hc_patients, k = kk)
  mean(cluster::silhouette(cl, dist_mat)[, "sil_width"])
})

sil_df <- tibble(k = k_grid, silhouette = sil_mean)

ggplot(sil_df, aes(k, silhouette)) +
  geom_line() +
  geom_point() +
  labs(
    x = "Number of clusters (k)",
    y = "Mean silhouette",
    title = "Choosing k for hierarchical clustering (Ward.D2)"
  ) +
  theme_bw()








In this example, the value \(k=3\) is supported both by the simulated biological design and by inspection of the dendrogram structure, where three major branches become apparent at a meaningful separation height.


8.8.7 Stability Assessment
A visually convincing dendrogram does not guarantee that the clustering structure is robust. Stability analysis evaluates whether the identified patient clusters persist under small perturbations of the data.
One common approach is bootstrap resampling. Patients are repeatedly sampled with replacement, hierarchical clustering is recomputed, and the similarity between bootstrap-derived clusters and the original clusters is quantified. The clusterboot procedure provides Jaccard similarity indices for each cluster, indicating how consistently each patient group reappears across resamples.
Clusters with high Jaccard values can be interpreted with greater confidence, as they represent reproducible structure rather than noise-driven artefacts. In high-dimensional genomic data, where random variation can easily generate spurious groupings, stability analysis serves as an essential safeguard against overinterpretation.
The Jaccard similarity values reported above quantify how consistently each cluster is recovered across bootstrap resamples. Values close to 1 indicate highly stable clusters, whereas values below approximately 0.6–0.7 suggest fragile structure that may not generalize under small perturbations of the data.

library(ComplexHeatmap)
library(circlize)
library(grid)

k <- 3

set.seed(1)
genes_show <- sample(colnames(expr_scaled), 60)
mat_show <- expr_scaled[, genes_show, drop = FALSE]

# Row annotation (known subtype)
ha <- rowAnnotation(
  Group = ann$Group,
  col = list(
    Group = c(
      "A_IFN"    = "#00BFC4",
      "B_Inflam" = "#F8766D",
      "C_Metab"  = "#619CFF"
    )
  ),
  annotation_name_side = "top"
)

# Heatmap colors for z-scores (scaled expression)
col_fun <- colorRamp2(c(-2, 0, 2), c("#2C7BB6", "#F7F7F7", "#D7191C"))

ht <- Heatmap(
  mat_show,
  name = "z",
  col = col_fun,

  # IMPORTANT: fixed dendrogram + numeric row_split
  cluster_rows = as.dendrogram(hc_patients),
  row_split = k,                     # <-- cut the dendrogram into k slices

  cluster_columns = TRUE,
  row_gap = unit(2.5, "mm"),
  show_row_names = FALSE,
  column_names_rot = 90,
  column_names_gp = gpar(fontsize = 8),

  left_annotation = ha,

  heatmap_legend_param = list(
    title = "Scaled expression (z)",
    at = c(-2, -1, 0, 1, 2),
    labels = c("≤ -2", "-1", "0", "+1", "≥ +2")
  ),

  column_title = "Patient clustering (Ward.D2) — k = 3 boxed clusters + subtype annotation",
  column_title_gp = gpar(fontsize = 14, fontface = "bold")
)

ht_drawn <- draw(ht, merge_legends = TRUE)

# Draw a rectangle around each split (slice)
for (i in seq_len(k)) {
  vp <- paste0("z_heatmap_body_", i, "_1")
  if (grid::seekViewport(vp, recording = FALSE)) {
    grid.rect(
      x = 0.5, y = 0.5, width = 1, height = 1,
      gp = gpar(col = "#111111", lwd = 2.2, fill = NA)
    )
    upViewport()
  }
}







# Colors represent gene-wise z-scores (after scaling each gene across patients):
# red = above that gene’s mean, blue = below, white ≈ mean.

Here the heatmap shows, in a single view, how patients relate to one another and how gene expression varies across them under Ward.D2 hierarchical clustering. Each row corresponds to a patient, ordered according to the dendrogram so that patients with similar overall expression profiles appear next to each other. The tree is cut at \(k=3\), and the three resulting groups are outlined with black boxes to make the partition visually explicit. Columns represent a subset of genes selected for readability, and their ordering reveals blocks of genes that tend to behave similarly across patients.
Colors represent gene-wise standardized expression values ( \(\mathbf{z}\)-scores). Red indicates that a gene is expressed above its average level across patients, blue indicates expression below the average, and white corresponds to values close to the mean. Because scaling was performed separately for each gene, the heatmap reflects relative up- or down-regulation within that gene rather than absolute abundance. In other words, a red cell does not mean “high expression in absolute terms,” but rather “higher expression in this patient compared to the cohort average for that gene.”
The annotation bar on the left indicates the known simulated subtype (A_IFN, B_Inflam, C_Metab). The alignment between the boxed clusters and the annotation colors is striking: each cluster corresponds almost entirely to a single subtype. This indicates that the hierarchical procedure has successfully recovered the embedded structure of the data.
More importantly, each cluster is characterized by a distinct pattern of coordinated gene expression. Within each boxed region, certain groups of genes appear consistently up-regulated (red) while the same genes are down-regulated (blue) in the other clusters. This pattern reflects subtype-specific molecular programs. For example, a block of genes that is red in one cluster and blue in the others suggests that those genes are preferentially activated in that patient group. Because scaling is gene-wise, these differences represent relative activation within each subtype rather than global shifts in overall expression levels.
The fact that the identity of “highly expressed” genes changes across clusters is precisely what drives the separation in the dendrogram. Clustering groups patients based on similarity of their multivariate expression profiles; if different subsets of genes are up-regulated in different patient groups, their global expression vectors become distinct. In this sense, the heatmap makes visible the mechanism underlying the clustering: each subtype is defined not by a single gene, but by coordinated shifts in expression across gene modules. These subtype-specific expression signatures generate the distances that the hierarchical algorithm uses to build the tree.

title: 9  Interpretable AI
text:
10 Introduction
In previous sections of the book, we learned how to perform supervised learning techniques and how to predict continuous or categorical outcomes using explanatory features and models such as OLS, LASSO, Ridge, Elastic Net, decision trees, random forests, XGBoost, and neural networks.
In this chapter, we examine how interpretability techniques help us understand not only the predictive performance of such models, but also what their parameters, structures, and prediction patterns mean. In addition, for models whose internal structure is more complex—such as random forests, gradient boosting models, Bayesian trees, and neural networks—we introduce techniques that help open the black box and translate model behavior into forms more accessible to human reasoning.
crumbs: 9  Interpretable AI

title: 9  Interpretable AI
text:
12.1 Interpretable AI
Interpretability in artificial intelligence refers to the capacity to render the behavior of a predictive model intelligible to human agents. In scientific, medical, and regulatory settings, predictive accuracy alone does not suffice. Models are embedded in inferential arguments, decision processes, and institutional accountability structures. Their outputs must therefore be accompanied by representations that allow examination, comparison, and reasoned critique.
Interpretability is relational and not a purely intrinsic property of an algorithm. A model is interpretable relative to a given audience, a specific decision context, and a defined epistemic objective. What constitutes an adequate explanation in methodological research may differ from what is required in clinical practice or policy evaluation. For this reason, interpretability must be understood simultaneously as a technical problem and as a problem of structured communication. Interpretability functions as a bridge between technical and non-technical personnel, as shown in Figure 12.1.






Figure 12.1: Conceptual diagram illustrating interpretability as a mediating structure between predictive models and human interpretation. Complex model outputs are translated into explanations, comparisons, and evaluations within a specific context, for a defined audience, and relative to an epistemic objective. The figure highlights the dependence of interpretability on audience literacy, symbolic logic, and domain-specific settings such as scientific research, clinical practice, and policy decision-making.
crumbs: 9  Interpretable AI

title: 9  Interpretable AI
text:
12.2 The context of communication
Every explanation presupposes a communicative structure. There is a system that generates signals, a representation of those signals, and an agent who interprets them within a conceptual framework. A predictive model encodes relationships between predictors and outcomes in a formal structure. However, this structure is typically not expressed in a form directly accessible to human reasoning. It may be embedded in a large collection of trees, a high-dimensional parameter vector, or a posterior distribution over functions.
Interpretability methods function as translation mechanisms. They construct secondary representations of a trained model in order to expose selected aspects of its internal structure or external behavior. These representations do not reproduce the full complexity of the model. Instead, they selectively preserve features such as predictor relevance, interaction strength, marginal effects, structural stability, or uncertainty.
From the perspective of the fundamental problem of communication, no representation is transmitted without transformation. A model encodes structure in mathematical or algorithmic form; interpretability techniques decode and re-encode that structure into forms compatible with human conceptual systems. The adequacy of an interpretability method depends on whether it preserves the structural features that are epistemically relevant in the context of use.
crumbs: 9  Interpretable AI

title: 9  Interpretable AI
text:
12.3 Scientific communication
In scientific practice, models serve not only as predictive instruments but also as representational frameworks. A linear regression expresses relationships through coefficients under explicit distributional and structural assumptions. A logistic regression encodes associations in terms of log-odds. A decision tree expresses structure through recursive partitioning of the predictor space. Each modeling framework carries an implicit theory of explanation grounded in its parameterization and assumptions.
Classical statistical models were often selected in part because their parameters possessed direct interpretative meaning. With the development of modern machine learning algorithms—such as random forests, gradient boosting machines, and neural networks—the emphasis shifted toward predictive performance in complex and high-dimensional settings. As model structure became more intricate, interpretability increasingly required dedicated methodological development. Models became black boxes, and the aim of this chapter is to make the main interpretive strategies explicit, including their assumptions, their limitations, and the kinds of representational objects they produce.
Interpretability procedures may therefore be regarded as meta-modeling operations. They take a fitted model as input and derive structured summaries of its behavior under controlled perturbations or structural inspection, often through visual representations designed to support scrutiny and comparison.
crumbs: 9  Interpretable AI

title: 9  Interpretable AI
text:
12.4 Models and representations as communication
Formally, a supervised learning model can be described as a function
\(g : \mathcal{X} \rightarrow \mathcal{Y}\),
where \(\mathcal{X}\) denotes the predictor space and \(\mathcal{Y}\) the response space. In practice, the learned mapping is rarely available in closed analytical form. Instead, it is encoded in computational structures: regression coefficients, weighted sums, collections of trees, boosting iterations, neural layers, or posterior samples.
Interpretability techniques construct alternative representations of this mapping. These may emphasize the relative influence of predictors, the presence of interaction effects, the shape of marginal response functions, or the stability of structural features across model realizations. Each such representation abstracts from certain aspects of the original mapping while preserving others. The design of interpretability methods therefore involves explicit trade-offs between fidelity to the fitted model, robustness to sampling variability and noise, computational feasibility in high dimensions, and cognitive clarity for a target audience.
A useful way to formalize this point is to view interpretability as producing a representation \(\mathcal{R}\) from a model \(g\) and data \(D\) through a transformation operator \(\mathcal{T}\):
\(\mathcal{T}(g, D) \mapsto \mathcal{R}\).
The representation \(\mathcal{R}\) can take multiple forms, including scalar summaries (importance scores), structured objects (interaction matrices), functional summaries (marginal effect curves), or geometric objects (networks, embeddings of proximity structure). The evaluation of \(\mathcal{R}\) depends on whether it supports the epistemic objective at hand—explanation, auditing, validation, or decision support—given the literacy level and symbolic logic available to the audience.
crumbs: 9  Interpretable AI

title: 9  Interpretable AI
text:
13.1 Model-Dependent Methods

13.1.1 Linear Models: OLS, LASSO, Ridge, Elastic Net
Model-dependent interpretability is most transparent in linear models, because the fitted structure is directly expressed through a coefficient vector. In this setting, each coefficient represents the expected change in the outcome associated with a one-unit increase in a predictor, holding the remaining predictors fixed. Since the predictors were preprocessed consistently, the coefficient magnitudes can also be compared as relative measures of influence within the fitted model.

13.1.1.1 Ordinary Least Squares (OLS)
We begin with the ordinary least squares (OLS) model. The code below reads the saved OLS object, retrieves the coefficient table stored during model fitting, and selects the ten coefficients with the largest absolute magnitude. This provides a compact summary of the strongest additive effects in the unpenalized linear specification.

# ===============================================================
# OLS coefficient inspection (lung_sim_complete example)
# ===============================================================

models_dir <- "/Users/danilosarti/Documents/ai_health_book/models/lung_sim_complete"

ols_obj <- readRDS(file.path(models_dir, "ols_small.rds"))

coef_ols_tbl <- ols_obj$coef_tbl

coef_ols_ranked <- coef_ols_tbl %>%
  dplyr::filter(term != "(Intercept)") %>%
  dplyr::arrange(desc(abs_estimate)) %>%
  dplyr::select(term, estimate, std.error, statistic, p.value, abs_estimate)

coef_ols_ranked

# A tibble: 5 × 6
  term     estimate std.error statistic  p.value abs_estimate
  <chr>       <dbl>     <dbl>     <dbl>    <dbl>        <dbl>
1 ph.ecog   -54.8        8.35    -6.56  6.72e-10       54.8  
2 wt.loss   -42.8        4.14   -10.3   1.32e-19       42.8  
3 ph.karno   39.2        8.14     4.82  3.24e- 6       39.2  
4 sex_male   -2.96       3.95    -0.750 4.54e- 1        2.96 
5 age        -0.725      3.87    -0.187 8.52e- 1        0.725


The OLS coefficient table summarizes the strongest additive effects in the unpenalized linear model fitted to the simulated lung cancer dataset. The largest coefficients in absolute magnitude correspond to the clinical status variables ph.ecog (−54.8) and wt.loss (−42.8), indicating that poorer performance status and greater weight loss are strongly associated with shorter predicted survival time. Both variables capture aspects of patient deterioration and disease burden, so their strong negative association with the outcome is consistent with the structure embedded in the simulated data-generating process. By contrast, the Karnofsky performance score ph.karno appears with a large positive coefficient (39.2), reflecting the fact that higher functional capacity is associated with longer expected survival time.
The remaining predictors have considerably smaller estimated effects. The coefficient for sex_male (−2.96) suggests a weak negative association with survival time, while the effect of age (−0.73) is minimal once functional status variables are included in the model. Both predictors also show large p-values, indicating substantial uncertainty in their estimated contribution within this linear specification. Overall, the OLS model captures a clinically interpretable additive structure dominated by measures of patient condition and functional status. However, because OLS assumes a purely linear and additive relationship and does not include regularization, the resulting coefficients may still be sensitive to correlations among predictors and may fail to capture nonlinear patterns or interactions present in the underlying data-generating mechanism.


13.1.1.2 Penalized linear models: LASSO, Ridge, and Elastic Net
We now compare this unpenalized baseline with three regularized linear models: LASSO, Ridge, and Elastic Net. These methods preserve the same basic additive structure, but they modify the estimation procedure through penalization. Ridge shrinks all coefficients continuously toward zero, LASSO can set many coefficients exactly to zero, and Elastic Net combines both mechanisms.
The next code block reads the saved coefficient tables for the three penalized models, removes coefficients that were shrunk to zero, orders the remaining coefficients by absolute magnitude, and extracts the ten most important terms in each case. Since penalized regression does not naturally provide standard errors or p-values in the same way as OLS, the tables focus on the coefficient estimates themselves and their absolute size.

# ===============================================================
# Penalized linear models — coefficient inspection
# lung_sim_complete example
# ===============================================================

glmnet_obj <- readRDS(file.path(models_dir, "glmnet_small.rds"))

coef_lasso_tbl <- glmnet_obj$coef_lasso_tbl
coef_ridge_tbl <- glmnet_obj$coef_ridge_tbl
coef_enet_tbl  <- glmnet_obj$coef_enet_tbl

coef_lasso_ranked <- coef_lasso_tbl %>%
  dplyr::filter(estimate != 0) %>%
  dplyr::arrange(desc(abs_estimate)) %>%
  dplyr::select(term, estimate, abs_estimate)

coef_ridge_ranked <- coef_ridge_tbl %>%
  dplyr::filter(estimate != 0) %>%
  dplyr::arrange(desc(abs_estimate)) %>%
  dplyr::select(term, estimate, abs_estimate)

coef_enet_ranked <- coef_enet_tbl %>%
  dplyr::filter(estimate != 0) %>%
  dplyr::arrange(desc(abs_estimate)) %>%
  dplyr::select(term, estimate, abs_estimate)

coef_lasso_ranked

      term  estimate abs_estimate
1  ph.ecog -53.59112     53.59112
2  wt.loss -40.52776     40.52776
3 ph.karno  37.22477     37.22477

coef_ridge_ranked

      term    estimate abs_estimate
1  ph.ecog -50.3910516   50.3910516
2  wt.loss -40.4722700   40.4722700
3 ph.karno  40.1681138   40.1681138
4 sex_male  -2.9850627    2.9850627
5      age  -0.8697526    0.8697526

coef_enet_ranked

      term   estimate abs_estimate
1  ph.ecog -53.897104    53.897104
2  wt.loss -41.958996    41.958996
3 ph.karno  38.925372    38.925372
4 sex_male  -2.161977     2.161977


The three penalized models recover a highly consistent set of influential predictors in the lung cancer example. Across LASSO, Ridge, and Elastic Net, the clinical status variables ph.ecog, wt.loss, and ph.karno consistently appear with the largest coefficients in absolute magnitude. Poorer ECOG performance status (ph.ecog) and greater weight loss (wt.loss) are associated with shorter predicted survival time, while higher Karnofsky scores (ph.karno) are associated with longer expected survival time. These results mirror the structure observed in the OLS model and reinforce the central role of patient functional status and clinical deterioration in determining prognosis within the simulated data-generating process.
The main differences among the penalized models arise in the sparsity and shrinkage of the coefficients. LASSO produces the most compact representation, retaining only the three strongest predictors (ph.ecog, wt.loss, and ph.karno) and shrinking the remaining coefficients to zero. Ridge regression, by contrast, retains all predictors but shrinks them smoothly toward zero, resulting in a denser coefficient profile that still includes smaller effects such as sex_male and age. Elastic Net occupies an intermediate position: it preserves the dominant predictors and retains a small additional effect for sex_male, while still producing a relatively sparse representation. These patterns illustrate the central logic of regularization: Ridge stabilizes estimation through continuous shrinkage, LASSO performs variable selection, and Elastic Net balances both mechanisms. Predictors that remain large across all three models can therefore be interpreted as particularly stable signals in the predictive structure of the data.


13.1.1.3 Comparing coefficient structures across linear models
A useful way to summarize these differences is to compare the coefficients visually across models. The next code block combines the top coefficients from OLS, LASSO, Ridge, and Elastic Net into a single table and plots their estimates side by side. This makes it easier to see which predictors remain stable across models and how regularization changes the magnitude of the fitted effects.

# ===============================================================
# Compare coefficients across linear models
# lung_sim_complete example
# ===============================================================

coef_compare <- bind_rows(
  coef_ols_ranked %>% select(term, estimate) %>% mutate(model = "OLS"),
  coef_lasso_ranked %>% select(term, estimate) %>% mutate(model = "LASSO"),
  coef_ridge_ranked %>% select(term, estimate) %>% mutate(model = "Ridge"),
  coef_enet_ranked %>% select(term, estimate) %>% mutate(model = "Elastic Net")
)

coef_compare %>%
  ggplot(aes(x = reorder(term, abs(estimate)), y = estimate, color = model)) +
  geom_point(size = 3) +
  coord_flip() +
  labs(
    title = "Coefficient comparison across linear models",
    x = "",
    y = "Coefficient estimate"
  ) +
  theme_bw(base_size = 12)








The comparison plot makes the effect of regularization visually explicit. OLS produces the largest coefficient magnitudes overall, reflecting the absence of penalization. Ridge shrinks coefficients more smoothly toward zero while retaining all predictors, resulting in a denser but more conservative representation. LASSO produces the sparsest model, keeping only the three dominant predictors—ph.ecog, wt.loss, and ph.karno—and shrinking the remaining coefficients exactly to zero. Elastic Net occupies an intermediate position: like LASSO, it preserves the strongest predictors, but it also retains a small coefficient for sex_male, reflecting its balance between shrinkage and variable selection.
Several terms remain strikingly stable across models. The variables ph.ecog, wt.loss, and ph.karno consistently appear with the largest coefficients in absolute magnitude, reinforcing the conclusion that patient functional status and clinical deterioration are the main structural drivers of predicted survival time in this example. By contrast, sex_male appears only in OLS, Ridge, and Elastic Net, while age is retained only in OLS and Ridge with very small magnitude, suggesting that these variables provide weaker or less stable signal once regularization is introduced.
This sequence of outputs illustrates the essence of model-dependent interpretability in linear settings. The explanatory structure is encoded directly in the coefficient vector, but its final form depends strongly on the fitting procedure. OLS offers the clearest unpenalized additive baseline. Ridge yields a dense but stabilized representation. LASSO produces a sparse explanatory narrative focused only on the strongest predictors. Elastic Net lies between these two extremes, retaining the dominant variables while allowing limited additional structure. Together, these models provide an interpretable bridge between classical regression and more flexible predictive methods.
This coefficient-based perspective is especially powerful when the internal structure of the model is itself meaningful, as in linear and regularized linear regression. However, many modern predictive models do not expose their logic through a compact parameter vector. In those settings, interpretability must often be constructed from model behavior rather than read directly from model structure, motivating the move to tree-based summaries and model-agnostic methods.

title: 9  Interpretable AI
text:
13.2 Decision trees

13.2.1 Recursive partitioning as explanation
Beyond linear models, decision trees provide another important example of model-dependent interpretability. In a regression or classification tree, the fitted model is expressed as a sequence of recursive partitioning rules applied to the predictor space. Each internal node corresponds to a split on one predictor, and each terminal node corresponds to a predicted outcome for observations satisfying the sequence of conditions along that branch.
This makes single trees intrinsically interpretable. Unlike linear models, where interpretation is carried by a vector of coefficients, trees encode explanation through a rule-based structure. A fitted tree can be read as a hierarchical set of conditional statements: if a patient satisfies one condition, the model follows one branch; otherwise it follows another. In this sense, the tree itself becomes an explanatory object. Its structure reveals which variables are used first, which thresholds define meaningful partitions, and how the predictor space is divided into clinically distinct subgroups.
In the lung cancer example used in this chapter, a regression tree may begin by splitting patients according to performance status (ph.ecog) or weight loss (wt.loss), two variables that strongly influence predicted survival time. Subsequent splits may refine the prediction using variables such as Karnofsky score (ph.karno), sex, or age. These partitions define subgroups of patients with different expected survival profiles. Variables appearing in early splits often play a particularly influential role in the partitioning strategy of the tree, although this should not be confused with a formal global measure of variable importance.
Tree ensembles such as Random Forests, Gradient Boosting, and Bayesian Additive Regression Trees extend this idea by aggregating large numbers of trees. Individual trees in these ensembles are usually not interpreted directly, because the predictive model is distributed across hundreds of trees. Instead, interpretation relies on structural summaries derived from the ensemble, such as variable importance measures based on split frequency, impurity reduction, or prediction degradation under variable perturbation. These summaries remain model-dependent because they arise directly from the internal architecture of the fitted tree-based model.
At this stage it is useful to distinguish these embedded structural summaries from model-agnostic interpretability techniques. Some interpretability tools can operate in both settings. For example, the vivid framework combines measures of variable importance and interaction strength that can be derived either from model-specific structures or from model-agnostic procedures such as permutation and partial dependence. Later in this chapter we will examine these approaches in more detail. For now, the focus remains on the structural interpretability naturally provided by single trees and tree-based models.

# ===============================================================
# Load saved CART model
# ===============================================================

models_dir <- "/Users/danilosarti/Documents/ai_health_book/models/lung_sim_complete"

tree_obj <- readRDS(file.path(models_dir, "tree_reg_small.rds"))

tree_fit <- tree_obj$model
tree_cp_tbl <- as.data.frame(tree_obj$cp_table)
tree_best_cp <- tree_obj$best_cp

library(rpart.plot)

rpart.plot::rpart.plot(
  tree_fit,
  type = 2,
  extra = 101,
  fallen.leaves = TRUE,
  under = TRUE,
  cex = 0.7

According to the figure above, the regression tree partitions the patient population through a sequence of simple decision rules, each based on a single predictor and threshold. The first split occurs on ph.ecog, which represents the ECOG performance status of the patient. This initial partition separates patients with relatively better functional status from those with worse performance status, producing two groups with markedly different predicted survival times. Patients with poorer ECOG status fall into a branch with substantially lower predicted survival, while those with better performance status move to a branch associated with longer expected survival.
Within these branches, the tree further refines predictions using variables related to patient condition, particularly wt.loss and ph.karno. For example, among patients with relatively good ECOG status, weight loss becomes the next important partitioning variable, separating individuals with greater weight loss—who tend to have shorter predicted survival—from those with more stable weight. In another branch, the Karnofsky score (ph.karno) is used to refine predictions, with higher values indicating better functional capacity and therefore longer expected survival time.
Overall, the structure of the tree reveals a clinically interpretable hierarchy of predictors. Functional status measured by ECOG appears as the most influential variable, followed by indicators of physical deterioration such as weight loss and Karnofsky score. Rather than relying on a single additive equation, the tree divides the population into clinically meaningful subgroups with distinct survival profiles. In this way, the regression tree provides an intuitive representation of how combinations of clinical variables jointly shape predicted outcomes.


13.2.2 Tree ensembles: embedded structural summaries

13.2.2.1 Random Forests
Random forests replace the single-tree logic of direct rule reading with an ensemble-based logic of aggregated structural summaries. Instead of interpreting a single sequence of decision rules, interpretation focuses on how predictive influence is distributed across many trees. In practice, this is commonly examined through variable importance measures and, when relevant, through summaries of interaction structure across the ensemble.
In this chapter we use two complementary perspectives. First, we examine the embedded importance information stored directly in the fitted random forest model. This provides a model-dependent summary of how strongly each predictor contributed to the construction of the ensemble during training. Second, we later use the vivid framework to construct a joint representation of variable importance and interaction strength, allowing us to move from simple rankings toward a more structured view of the predictive mechanisms captured by the forest.
The next chunk loads the fitted random forest model and extracts its embedded variable importance scores. These values provide a first structural summary of the ensemble before we move to richer visual summaries such as VIVI matrices and interaction networks.

# ===============================================================
# Random Forest embedded importance
# ===============================================================

rf_obj <- readRDS(file.path(models_dir, "rf_reg_small.rds"))
rf_fit <- rf_obj$model

rf_vimp_tbl <- tibble(
  term = names(rf_fit$variable.importance),
  importance = as.numeric(rf_fit$variable.importance)
) %>%
  arrange(desc(importance))

rf_vimp_tbl

# A tibble: 5 × 2
  term     importance
  <chr>         <dbl>
1 ph.ecog     970839.
2 ph.karno    799544.
3 wt.loss     496534.
4 age          90357.
5 sex_male     14450.


The table above reports the embedded variable importance values produced by the fitted random forest. Since this model was trained using impurity-based importance, the scores summarize how much each predictor contributed, across the ensemble, to reductions in node impurity during tree construction. Predictors with larger values therefore played a stronger role in the recursive partitioning strategy of the forest.
In this example, the variables ph.ecog and ph.karno appear as the most influential predictors, followed by wt.loss. These variables represent different aspects of patient functional status and physical deterioration, which is consistent with the clinical logic already observed in the linear models and in the regression tree. By contrast, age and sex_male receive substantially smaller importance values, indicating that they play a more limited role in the predictive structure of the forest.
Unlike the coefficient-based interpretation of linear models, these importance values do not indicate the direction of the effect. They identify which predictors contributed most strongly to prediction accuracy, but they do not tell us whether increasing a predictor raises or lowers the expected outcome. For that reason, tree-based importance should be interpreted as a measure of structural relevance rather than as a signed effect size. A simple graphical summary can help highlight the dominant predictors more clearly.
A simple graphical summary helps identify the dominant predictors more clearly.

rf_vimp_tbl %>%
  slice_max(order_by = importance, n = 15) %>%
  ggplot(aes(x = reorder(term, importance), y = importance)) +
  geom_col() +
  coord_flip() +
  labs(
    title = "Random Forest embedded variable importance",
    x = "",
    y = "Importance"
  ) +
  theme_bw(base_size = 12)








Embedded importance, however, still provides only a partial view of the model. It summarizes marginal structural relevance, but it does not directly show whether important variables are acting mainly through additive effects or through interactions. To study this broader structure, we now turn to a VIVI representation using the vivid package.


13.2.2.2 Gradient boosting models (XGBoost)
Gradient boosting models extend the tree-based logic in a different way from random forests. Instead of building many trees independently and averaging their predictions, boosting constructs trees sequentially. Each new tree is trained to improve the errors made by the previous ensemble, so that predictive structure is accumulated stage by stage. Interpretation therefore focuses not on a single tree, but on how predictive influence is distributed across the boosting process.
As with random forests, we begin by examining model-dependent structural summaries. For XGBoost, embedded importance measures are derived from the fitted boosting ensemble itself. These importance scores summarize how strongly each predictor contributed to the boosted trees according to criteria such as improvement in the objective function, frequency of use in splits, or the number of observations affected by those splits. In the present chapter, we focus on Gain, which measures the average contribution of a variable to improving model fit across the ensemble.
The next chunk loads the fitted XGBoost model and extracts its embedded variable importance values. These provide a first structural summary of how the boosted model distributed predictive work across the clinical predictors.
In an analougous manner the following codes extract variable importance from XGboost models.

# ===============================================================
# XGBoost embedded importance
# ===============================================================
library(xgboost)
xgb_obj <- readRDS(file.path(models_dir, "xgb_reg_small.rds"))
xgb_fit <- xgb_obj$model

xgb_vimp_tbl <- xgb.importance(model = xgb_fit) %>%
  as_tibble() %>%
  arrange(desc(Gain))

xgb_vimp_tbl

# A tibble: 5 × 4
  Feature     Gain  Cover Frequency
  <chr>      <dbl>  <dbl>     <dbl>
1 ph.ecog  0.460   0.164     0.126 
2 ph.karno 0.339   0.292     0.307 
3 wt.loss  0.183   0.376     0.370 
4 age      0.0158  0.148     0.172 
5 sex_male 0.00195 0.0198    0.0248



xgb_vimp_tbl %>%
  ggplot(aes(x = reorder(Feature, Gain), y = Gain)) +
  geom_col() +
  coord_flip() +
  labs(
    title = "XGBoost embedded variable importance",
    x = "",
    y = "Gain"
  ) +
  theme_bw(base_size = 12)








The table above reports the embedded variable importance values produced by the fitted XGBoost model. In this setting, the most relevant summary is Gain, which quantifies how much each predictor contributed, on average, to improving the objective function when it was used in the boosted trees. A predictor with a larger Gain value therefore contributed more strongly to the predictive performance of the ensemble than a predictor with a smaller value. The table also allows a direct numerical ranking of the predictors, making it possible to compare how much predictive work was allocated to each variable within the boosting process.
In the present lung cancer example, the highest Gain values are concentrated in the clinical status variables, especially ph.ecog, ph.karno, and wt.loss, which appear as the three dominant predictors in the boosted model. This indicates that most of the predictive improvement achieved by the XGBoost ensemble is driven by variables related to patient functional status and physical deterioration. By contrast, age and sex_male contribute much smaller gain values, indicating that their role in improving the objective function is comparatively limited. This numerical pattern is consistent with the results already observed in the linear models, the regression tree, and the random forest, where the same three variables also emerged as the main predictive drivers. As with random forests, however, XGBoost importance values do not indicate the direction of an effect. They summarize structural contribution to predictive improvement, but do not directly tell us whether increasing a predictor leads to higher or lower predicted survival time. For that reason, XGBoost importance should be interpreted as a measure of structural relevance rather than as a signed effect size.



13.2.3 From embedded importance to model-agnostic functional summaries
Embedded importance measures derived from tree ensembles provide useful structural summaries of how predictors contribute to model construction. These summaries reveal which predictors were most influential in building the ensemble, but they do not directly show how predictions change as individual predictors vary across their observed ranges. In other words, variable importance identifies which variables matter for prediction, but it does not explain how those variables influence the predicted outcome or whether their effects remain stable across different observations.
To investigate these functional relationships we turn to model-agnostic interpretability methods. These techniques treat the fitted model as a prediction function and study how predictions respond to controlled changes in the input variables. Because they rely only on the prediction mechanism and not on the internal structure of the model, these methods can be applied to any supervised learning algorithm, including tree ensembles and neural networks.
In the analyses that follow, we introduce a sequence of model-agnostic interpretability tools that progressively reveal different aspects of model behavior. We begin with permutation-based measures of global variable importance. We then examine partial dependence plots and individual conditional expectation curves, which describe how model predictions vary as predictors change. Finally, we return to the VIVI framework, which combines importance and interaction structure into a unified representation.
These techniques allow us to move from structural summaries of model construction toward functional explanations of model behavior. In the present example they are applied to three predictive models with increasing structural flexibility: a Random Forest, an XGBoost model, and a Neural Network. Together, these visualizations provide a richer picture of how the clinical predictors influence predicted survival time in the simulated lung cancer dataset.


13.2.4 Global variable importance

13.2.4.1 Permutation importance
Permutation importance provides a model-agnostic way to quantify how strongly a fitted predictive model relies on each predictor variable. The central idea is simple: if a predictor is important for prediction, then breaking the association between that predictor and the outcome should substantially degrade predictive performance.
Let \(\hat{g}\) denote the fitted prediction function and let \(w(\hat{g}, D)\) represent a performance score computed on dataset \(D\), such as RMSE, MAE, or classification error. For a predictor \(X_r\), we construct a perturbed dataset \(D^{\pi_r}\) by randomly permuting the values of \(X_r\) while leaving all other predictors unchanged. The fitted model is then evaluated on this perturbed dataset.
Repeating the permutation \(R\) times yields the permutation importance score
\[
imp_r
=
w(\hat{g}, D)
-
\frac{1}{R}
\sum_{k=1}^{R}
w(\hat{g}, D^{\pi_r,k})
\]
This quantity measures how much predictive performance deteriorates when the information contained in predictor \(X_r\) is destroyed. Large values indicate that the model relies heavily on that predictor, whereas values close to zero suggest that the predictor plays a limited role in the predictive mechanism.
Permutation importance has several advantages. Because it relies only on the prediction function \(\hat{g}\), it can be applied to any supervised learning model, including tree ensembles, boosting models, and neural networks. It also allows a direct comparison of variable importance across different algorithms within the same predictive task.
However, permutation importance must be interpreted carefully when predictors are correlated. Permuting one variable may disrupt the joint dependence structure between predictors, creating combinations of feature values that are rare or unrealistic in the observed data. In such cases the resulting scores should be interpreted as measures of model reliance rather than as causal measures of variable influence.



13.2.5 Interaction diagnostics
Variable importance describes how strongly individual predictors contribute to prediction, but it does not reveal whether predictors act independently or jointly. Many predictive models capture interaction effects, meaning that the influence of one predictor depends on the value of another.
Model-agnostic interaction diagnostics often rely on partial dependence functions. Let \(f_r(x_r)\) and \(f_s(x_s)\) denote the univariate partial dependence functions for predictors \(X_r\) and \(X_s\), and let \(f_{rs}(x_r,x_s)\) denote the bivariate partial dependence surface. If the model is additive in these variables, the joint effect can be approximated by the sum of the marginal effects.
A widely used interaction diagnostic is the Friedman–Popescu \(H\)-statistic, defined as
\[
H_{rs}^2
=
\frac{
\sum_{i=1}^{n}
\left[
f_{rs}(x_{ir},x_{is})
-
f_r(x_{ir})
-
f_s(x_{is})
\right]^2
}{
\sum_{i=1}^{n}
f_{rs}(x_{ir},x_{is})^2
}
\]
Large values of \(H_{rs}\) indicate strong departures from additivity, suggesting that the predictive effect of one variable depends on the value of another. Interaction diagnostics therefore complement variable importance by revealing whether predictive influence arises mainly through marginal effects or through joint relationships among predictors.

13.2.5.1 VIVI: Variable importance and interaction structure
The VIVI framework provides a joint representation of variable importance and interaction strength. Instead of examining these components separately, the method summarizes them in a matrix-like visualization in which diagonal elements represent the marginal importance of each predictor, while off-diagonal elements represent the strength of pairwise interactions between predictors.
Unlike embedded importance measures derived directly from tree-based algorithms, VIVI can be computed in a model-agnostic way. The method relies on partial dependence calculations to estimate both marginal effects and interaction structure, allowing the same interpretability framework to be applied across very different modeling approaches.
In the present example we compute VIVI summaries for the Random Forest, XGBoost, and Neural Network models. This comparison allows us to examine how each model distributes predictive influence across the clinical predictors and whether interactions between predictors play a substantial role in the prediction of survival time.












































The VIVI representations show a highly consistent predictive structure across the three fitted models. In all cases, the variables ph.ecog, wt.loss, and ph.karno form the main core of the model, appearing with the largest marginal importance values. This indicates that patient functional status and clinical deterioration are the dominant drivers of predicted survival time in the simulated lung cancer example. By contrast, age and sex_male appear with substantially lower importance, suggesting a more limited role in the predictive structure.
The interaction patterns are also informative. Across Random Forest, XGBoost, and Neural Network models, the strongest pairwise interactions are concentrated among ph.ecog, wt.loss, and ph.karno. In the Random Forest and XGBoost models, the interaction between wt.loss and ph.karno appears especially strong, while the interaction between ph.ecog and wt.loss is also consistently prominent. In the Neural Network, the interaction structure is slightly more centered on ph.ecog, which acts as a highly important variable connected strongly to both wt.loss and ph.karno. Taken together, these results suggest that the fitted models agree not only on the most important individual predictors, but also on the fact that prediction depends on their joint action rather than on purely additive effects.

13.2.6 Partial dependence and individual conditional expectation
Interpretability methods based on variable importance and interaction summaries provide information about which variables contribute most strongly to prediction. However, these summaries do not directly reveal the functional relationship learned by the model between predictors and the outcome. In other words, they identify the most influential variables, but they do not show how predicted values change as those variables vary. To understand this functional behavior, we turn to model-agnostic techniques that analyze the response surface of the fitted model itself. Two of the most widely used tools for this purpose are Partial Dependence Plots (PDP) and Individual Conditional Expectation (ICE) curves.
Consider a predictive model \(\hat{f}(\mathbf{x})\) trained on a set of predictors \(\mathbf{x} = (x_1, x_2, \ldots, x_p)\). Suppose we wish to understand the effect of a subset of predictors \(\mathbf{x}_S \subseteq \mathbf{x}\), where \(S\) indexes a set of variables of interest, and let \(\mathbf{x}_C\) denote the remaining predictors. The partial dependence function is defined as the expected model prediction when the variables in \(S\) are fixed at specific values and the remaining predictors vary according to their empirical distribution:
\[
f_S(\mathbf{x}_S) = \mathbb{E}_{\mathbf{x}_C}\left[\hat{f}(\mathbf{x}_S, \mathbf{x}_C)\right].
\]
Because the joint distribution of predictors is typically unknown, this expectation is approximated empirically using the observed dataset. Given \(n\) observations, the partial dependence function can be estimated as
\[
\hat{f}_S(\mathbf{x}_S) = \frac{1}{n} \sum_{i=1}^{n} \hat{f}(\mathbf{x}_S, \mathbf{x}_{C,i}),
\]
where \(\mathbf{x}_{C,i}\) denotes the observed values of the complementary predictors for observation \(i\). Intuitively, this computation evaluates the model prediction repeatedly while fixing the variable of interest at a chosen value and averaging over all observed combinations of the remaining predictors. By repeating this process across a grid of values for \(\mathbf{x}_S\), we obtain the partial dependence curve, which describes the average predicted response as the predictor varies.
Partial dependence therefore provides a population-level view of the model’s learned relationship between predictors and the outcome. The resulting curves reveal whether the model encodes approximately linear relationships, monotonic nonlinear patterns, or more complex functional shapes. Importantly, PDPs do not depend on the internal structure of the model and can therefore be applied to linear models, tree ensembles, neural networks, and other predictive algorithms.
However, partial dependence curves represent an average effect across all observations. When predictors interact strongly with other variables, averaging may conceal substantial heterogeneity in the individual responses. To address this limitation, Individual Conditional Expectation (ICE) curves examine the model prediction separately for each observation.
For a given observation \(i\), the ICE function is defined as
\[
\hat{f}^{(i)}_S(\mathbf{x}_S) = \hat{f}(\mathbf{x}_S, \mathbf{x}_{C,i}),
\]
which represents the predicted response when the predictor of interest varies while all other predictors are fixed at the values observed for that specific individual. Plotting this function for all observations produces a family of curves, each describing how the model prediction would change for a particular observation as the predictor varies.
ICE plots therefore reveal heterogeneity in predictor effects across the dataset. When the individual curves are roughly parallel, the predictor has a relatively homogeneous effect across observations, and the partial dependence curve provides a reliable summary of the relationship. When the curves diverge or intersect, the effect of the predictor depends on the values of other variables, indicating the presence of interactions.
The VIVI analysis revealed that the predictive structure of the models is dominated by three variables: ph.ecog, wt.loss, and ph.karno. These variables represent different aspects of patient functional status and physical deterioration, and they appear not only as the most important predictors across the Random Forest, XGBoost, and Neural Network models, but also as the variables most strongly involved in pairwise interactions. Having identified these key predictors, the next step is to examine how each of them influences the predicted outcome across its range of values.
While variable importance and interaction summaries describe which variables matter for prediction, they do not reveal how the prediction changes as those variables vary. Partial dependence plots address this question by describing how the model prediction changes, on average, as one predictor varies while the remaining predictors are averaged over their empirical distribution. In this way, PDPs provide a functional description of the learned relationship between predictors and the outcome.
In the present lung cancer example, partial dependence analysis focuses on ph.ecog, wt.loss, and ph.karno, allowing us to visualize how each model translates these clinical variables into predicted survival time. Because the same predictors are examined across Random Forest, XGBoost, and Neural Network models, the resulting curves also allow a comparison of how different algorithms approximate the same predictive relationship.
However, partial dependence curves summarize the average relationship across all observations. When predictors interact, averaging may hide important variation in the individual responses. Individual Conditional Expectation (ICE) curves address this limitation by plotting the predicted response for each observation separately as the predictor varies. Instead of a single average curve, ICE plots show a family of curves corresponding to individual patients.
When the ICE curves are roughly parallel, the predictor has a relatively homogeneous effect across observations and the partial dependence curve provides a good summary. When the curves diverge or cross, this suggests that the effect of the predictor varies depending on the values of other variables, indicating the presence of interactions. In the present case, this is particularly relevant because the VIVI analysis already indicated strong interactions among ph.ecog, wt.loss, and ph.karno.
Together, PDP and ICE analyses provide a complementary perspective on the fitted models. PDPs reveal the overall functional relationship learned by the model, while ICE curves reveal how that relationship varies across individuals. This combination allows us to move from structural summaries of the model toward a more detailed understanding of its predictive behavior.
The following chunks of code implement PDP and ICE for our example.

# ===============================================================
# PDP and ICE with vivid — setup
# ===============================================================

library(vivid)
library(dplyr)
library(keras)
library(grid)

vars_focus <- c("ph.ecog", "wt.loss", "ph.karno")

# ------------------------------------------------
# Custom predict functions in vivid format
# IMPORTANT: the argument name must be `data`
# ------------------------------------------------

pFun_rf <- function(fit, data, ...) {
  data <- as.data.frame(data)

  if ("time" %in% names(data)) {
    data <- dplyr::select(data, -time)
  }

  predict(fit, data = data)$predictions
}

pFun_xgb <- function(fit, data, ...) {
  data <- as.data.frame(data)

  if ("time" %in% names(data)) {
    data <- dplyr::select(data, -time)
  }

  feature_names <- xgb_obj$feature_names

  missing_cols <- setdiff(feature_names, names(data))
  if (length(missing_cols) > 0) {
    for (mc in missing_cols) {
      data[[mc]] <- 0
    }
  }

  data <- data[, feature_names, drop = FALSE]

  predict(fit, as.matrix(data))
}

pFun_nn <- function(fit, data, ...) {
  data <- as.data.frame(data)

  if ("time" %in% names(data)) {
    data <- dplyr::select(data, -time)
  }

  feature_names <- xgb_obj$feature_names

  missing_cols <- setdiff(feature_names, names(data))
  if (length(missing_cols) > 0) {
    for (mc in missing_cols) {
      data[[mc]] <- 0
    }
  }

  data <- data[, feature_names, drop = FALSE]
  data <- data.matrix(data)
  storage.mode(data) <- "double"

  as.numeric(fit$predict(data, verbose = 0))
}

 # load neural network model
nn_model <- keras::load_model_tf(nn_obj$model_path)

The PDP and ICE plots provide a functional view of how the models translate predictor values into predicted outcomes. In each panel, the horizontal axis represents the value of the predictor being varied, while the vertical axis shows the corresponding predicted survival time produced by the model. The thick black curve represents the partial dependence function, which averages the predicted response across all observations and therefore summarizes the overall relationship learned by the model. The colored curves correspond to individual conditional expectation (ICE) trajectories, each showing how the prediction would change for a specific patient if that predictor varied while the remaining variables were kept fixed at that patient’s observed values. When the ICE curves are roughly parallel, the effect of the predictor is relatively homogeneous across individuals; when the curves diverge or cross, this indicates that the predictor interacts with other variables in the model.
The PDP and ICE visualizations reveal a remarkably consistent functional structure across the three models. For ph.ecog, all algorithms learn a strong negative relationship with predicted survival time: as the ECOG performance score increases, the expected survival decreases sharply. This pattern is particularly clear in the Random Forest and XGBoost models, where the PDP curve shows step-like drops reflecting the tree-based partitioning structure. The neural network produces a smoother but qualitatively similar monotonic decline, indicating that worsening functional status is consistently associated with poorer predicted outcomes.
A similar decreasing relationship appears for wt.loss. Across the three models, larger weight loss is associated with progressively lower predicted survival. In the tree-based models the effect appears as piecewise decreases corresponding to splits in the ensemble, while the neural network again approximates the same relationship with a smooth nonlinear curve. The ICE curves also reveal moderate heterogeneity across individuals, suggesting that the magnitude of the effect depends on other patient characteristics.
By contrast, ph.karno shows the opposite pattern. Higher Karnofsky performance scores are associated with longer predicted survival times, producing a strong positive relationship in all models. As before, Random Forest and XGBoost display piecewise increases reflecting their recursive partitioning structure, while the neural network approximates a smooth increasing function. The ICE curves for this variable show larger dispersion than for the other predictors, indicating that the benefit associated with improved performance status may vary depending on the broader clinical context captured by the remaining predictors.
Taken together, the PDP and ICE analyses reinforce the central importance of functional status variables identified earlier by the VIVI analysis. Across three very different modeling approaches—Random Forest, XGBoost, and Neural Networks—the learned response surface consistently encodes poorer survival predictions for patients with worse ECOG scores or larger weight loss, and improved survival predictions for those with higher Karnofsky performance scores. These results suggest that the models are capturing clinically meaningful patterns rather than idiosyncratic algorithmic artifacts.



13.2.7 Generalized pairwise partial dependence plots
The univariate partial dependence and ICE plots examined above describe how the model prediction changes when a single predictor varies while the remaining predictors are averaged over their empirical distribution. These displays are useful for identifying the marginal functional form associated with each variable, but they do not directly reveal how pairs of predictors act jointly in the fitted response surface. When interpretability requires understanding interactions among predictors, multivariate visual summaries become necessary.
The vivid package provides a graphical tool designed for this purpose: the generalized partial dependence pairs plot, produced by the function pdpPairs(). This visualization extends the logic of univariate partial dependence by representing several layers of information within a single matrix-style display.
In these plots, the diagonal panels contain univariate partial dependence curves together with ICE trajectories, allowing each predictor to be examined individually. The upper triangular panels display bivariate partial dependence surfaces, which describe how the predicted response varies when two predictors change simultaneously while the remaining variables are averaged over their empirical distribution. These surfaces make it possible to detect interaction patterns such as curvature, threshold effects, or regions where the influence of one variable depends on the value of another. Finally, the lower triangular panels display the empirical distribution of the observed predictors, helping to assess whether the regions shown in the partial dependence surfaces are well supported by the available data.
In the present lung cancer example, this visualization is particularly useful because the previous VIVI analysis suggested that ph.ecog, wt.loss, and ph.karno form a strongly interacting set of predictors. The generalized pairs plot therefore allows us to study the joint structure of the learned response surface across the Random Forest, XGBoost, and Neural Network models.
The next figures display the generalized pairwise partial dependence plots for the three fitted models. Each matrix shows how the predicted survival time changes when pairs of predictors vary jointly, while the remaining predictors are averaged over the empirical distribution.
