13.2.8 Interpreting generalized pairwise partial dependence plots
The generalized pairwise partial dependence plots combine several complementary visual summaries in a single matrix display. Each panel of the matrix represents a different aspect of the learned predictive structure of the model. The diagonal panels show univariate partial dependence curves together with ICE trajectories, which describe how the predicted outcome changes when a single predictor varies while all other predictors are averaged over their empirical distribution. The thick black curve represents the average partial dependence function, while the colored curves correspond to the individual conditional expectation trajectories for different observations.
The upper triangular panels display bivariate partial dependence surfaces, where the color scale represents the predicted value of the response variable across combinations of two predictors. Warmer colors indicate larger predicted values of the outcome, while cooler colors correspond to smaller predicted values. These surfaces allow the analyst to detect interaction patterns, such as whether the effect of one variable becomes stronger or weaker depending on the value of another variable. Finally, the lower triangular panels show the empirical distribution of the predictors in the observed dataset. These panels provide an important reference because they indicate which regions of the predictor space are actually supported by the data and which regions correspond to extrapolation of the fitted model.
Across the three fitted models—Random Forest, XGBoost, and the Neural Network—the generalized pairwise partial dependence plots reveal a highly consistent structural pattern. The diagonal panels show that ph.ecog and wt.loss have a strong negative association with predicted survival time: as ECOG performance status worsens or as weight loss increases, the predicted survival time decreases substantially. In contrast, ph.karno exhibits the opposite pattern, with higher Karnofsky performance scores associated with increased predicted survival time. These relationships are monotonic in all three models, although their shapes differ slightly across algorithms.
The upper triangular panels reveal that these predictors also interact with one another in shaping the response surface. In particular, combinations of high ECOG scores and high weight loss correspond to regions of very low predicted survival time, as indicated by the deep blue regions of the surfaces. Conversely, combinations of high Karnofsky scores and low weight loss correspond to regions of high predicted survival time. These patterns indicate that the effect of one functional status measure is amplified when the others also reflect patient deterioration. The interaction structure therefore reflects a clinically coherent mechanism in which multiple indicators of declining physiological status jointly determine prognosis.
Although the general structure is consistent across the three models, some differences in smoothness and geometry can be observed. The tree-based models—Random Forest and XGBoost—produce surfaces that appear more piecewise and segmented, reflecting the recursive partitioning structure of tree ensembles. In contrast, the neural network produces smoother response surfaces and more gradual transitions across the predictor space, reflecting the continuous nonlinear functions learned by the network. Despite these architectural differences, the overall interaction patterns remain remarkably similar.
Taken together, these plots provide a coherent interpretation of the fitted models. The three predictors identified earlier by the VIVI analysis—ph.ecog, wt.loss, and ph.karno—form a tightly interacting group of variables that jointly determine predicted survival time. Rather than acting independently, these variables combine to define regions of the predictor space associated with markedly different prognostic outcomes. The consistency of these patterns across Random Forest, XGBoost, and Neural Network models strengthens the interpretation that the models are capturing a stable clinical relationship between functional status and survival rather than artifacts of a specific modeling approach.


13.2.9 Zen Partial Dependence Plots
While generalized pairwise partial dependence plots provide a comprehensive view of bivariate predictor relationships, they become increasingly difficult to read as the number of predictors grows. In a model with \(p\) predictors, the number of possible pairwise displays increases as \(p(p-1)/2\), which can quickly make full pairwise partial dependence grids visually impractical.
To address this problem, the vivid package provides Zen Partial Dependence Plots (ZPDPs) through the function pdpZen(). This visualization is based on the concept of zenplots, introduced by Hofert and Oldford, as a compact strategy for exploring many pairwise relationships in high-dimensional settings. Rather than displaying every possible pairwise panel, the method selects and orders the most relevant variable pairs and arranges them in a zig-zag sequence that preserves readability while emphasizing interpretively important structures.
Formally, let \(X_1, \dots, X_p\) denote the predictors in a fitted model \(\hat{f}\), and let \(I_{jk}\) denote a symmetric measure of pairwise interaction strength between predictors \(X_j\) and \(X_k\), such as the interaction values derived from the VIVI matrix. A Zen Partial Dependence Plot may be understood as a graph-based visualization built on a weighted undirected graph
\[
G = (V, E, W),
\]
where each vertex in \(V\) corresponds to a predictor, each edge in \(E\) corresponds to a pair of predictors, and the edge weights \(W_{jk}\) are given by the interaction strengths \(I_{jk}\).
The purpose of the zen layout is to construct a traversal path through the graph that prioritizes edges with larger weights, so that the displayed sequence of bivariate partial dependence plots focuses on the most important pairwise relationships in the model.
This idea is inspired by Eulerian path constructions in graph theory. In an Eulerian traversal, one visits edges of a graph in a systematic order. Zenplots adapt this principle to statistical graphics: instead of drawing all pairwise plots in a matrix, they construct a path through the most relevant variable pairs and display the corresponding bivariate partial dependence surfaces sequentially. In this way, the visualization becomes not only more compact, but also more explicitly guided by interaction strength.
For a given pair of predictors \(X_j\) and \(X_k\), the displayed bivariate partial dependence surface is based on the estimated function
\[
\hat{f}_{jk}(x_j, x_k)
=
\frac{1}{n}
\sum_{i=1}^{n}
\hat{f}(x_j, x_k, \mathbf{x}_{C,i}),
\]
where \(C\) denotes the set of all remaining predictors and \(\mathbf{x}_{C,i}\) are the observed values of those remaining predictors for observation \(i\).
Each panel of the Zen plot therefore displays the average fitted response over a grid of values of \((x_j, x_k)\) while averaging over the empirical distribution of the other predictors.
The key difference between a generalized pairwise PDP matrix and a Zen PDP is therefore not the mathematical definition of the bivariate partial dependence surface itself, but the selection and ordering of the displayed predictor pairs. The generalized pairwise PDP aims at exhaustive display over a selected subset of variables, whereas the Zen PDP aims at structured prioritization, concentrating visual attention on variable pairs that are most relevant according to the model’s interaction structure.
In practice, this makes Zen Partial Dependence Plots especially useful in settings where the predictor space is moderate or high dimensional and where a full matrix of pairwise PDPs would either exceed the available plotting space or dilute attention across too many low-information panels. In such cases, the Zen layout acts as a navigational device through the model’s most relevant interaction surfaces.

# Zen Partial Dependence Plot (ZPDP) — Random Forest
# ===============================================================

library(grid)

set.seed(1701)

pdpZen(
  data = train_baked,
  fit = rf_fit,
  response = "time",
  gridSize = 10,
  nmax = 500,
  predictFun = pFun_rf
)

13.2.10 Zen plot guided by interaction strength
A particularly useful feature of the Zen approach is that the traversal path can be defined explicitly from the interaction structure previously estimated by the VIVI framework. In this chapter, this creates a coherent interpretability pipeline: first we estimate variable importance and pairwise interaction strength using vivi(), then we use those interaction values to determine which bivariate partial dependence surfaces deserve visual emphasis.
Let \(M\) denote the VIVI matrix, where diagonal elements contain variable importance scores and off-diagonal elements contain pairwise interaction strengths. To construct a Zen path, one first removes the diagonal values and retains only the off-diagonal interaction entries. A threshold may then be imposed to exclude weak interactions. The remaining weighted graph is used to define a path through the strongest variable pairs.
This makes the Zen PDP especially valuable from a didactic perspective, because it does not merely show a compact collection of pairwise PDPs. Instead, it presents a graph-ordered sequence of the most relevant interaction surfaces, directly linking the visualization to the interaction ranking already identified in the VIVI analysis.
In the present lung cancer example, this means that predictor pairs involving ph.ecog, wt.loss, and ph.karno will tend to appear early in the Zen sequence whenever they exhibit the largest interaction values. The resulting display therefore acts as a focused continuation of the VIVI analysis: the heatmap and network identify the key interacting variables, and the Zen PDP reveals how the fitted response surface behaves over those pairs.


13.2.11 Interpreting the Zen Partial Dependence Plot
The Zen Partial Dependence Plot (Zen PDP) provides a compact visualization of the most relevant pairwise partial dependence surfaces in a predictive model. Rather than displaying all possible combinations of predictors in a full matrix, the Zenplot arranges a sequence of bivariate partial dependence surfaces along a path that prioritizes the strongest interactions identified in the model. Each panel therefore corresponds to one pair of predictors chosen along this interaction path.
In each panel, the horizontal and vertical axes represent the values of two predictors, while the color scale encodes the predicted value of the response variable. Warmer colors correspond to larger predicted survival times, whereas cooler colors correspond to lower predicted values. The surfaces therefore show how the model’s predicted outcome changes as two predictors vary simultaneously, while all remaining predictors are averaged over their empirical distribution.
The ordering of the panels reflects the interaction structure identified earlier through the VIVI analysis. The path used here was constructed from the strongest pairwise interactions in the Random Forest model, so variables that interact strongly appear repeatedly along the sequence of panels. In the present lung cancer example, the most prominent predictors are ph.ecog, ph.karno, and wt.loss, which represent different aspects of patient functional status and physical deterioration. As expected, these variables dominate the interaction path and therefore appear prominently in the Zen PDP.
The surfaces themselves reveal how these variables combine to shape predicted survival time. Panels involving ph.ecog show a clear gradient in which higher ECOG scores—indicating worse performance status—are associated with lower predicted survival time. Similarly, surfaces involving wt.loss display decreasing predictions as weight loss increases, reflecting the negative prognostic role of clinical deterioration. By contrast, panels involving ph.karno show the opposite pattern: higher Karnofsky scores correspond to improved predicted survival outcomes. When these predictors vary jointly, the color gradients become more pronounced, indicating that combinations of poor ECOG status and substantial weight loss produce the lowest predicted survival values, while high Karnofsky scores combined with low weight loss correspond to the most favorable predictions.
Compared with the generalized pairwise PDP matrix presented earlier, the Zen PDP is intentionally selective. Its goal is not to represent every possible interaction, but rather to guide interpretation toward the most informative regions of the predictor space. By following a path through the strongest interactions, the Zen PDP provides a concise visual summary of the interaction structure learned by the model.
From a broader interpretability perspective, the Zen PDP can be viewed as the final step in a sequence of interpretive tools. Variable importance measures identify which predictors matter most for prediction. VIVI summaries reveal which predictors interact with one another. Univariate partial dependence plots describe how individual predictors influence the response on average. Generalized pairwise PDP matrices display complete sets of interaction surfaces. The Zen PDP, in turn, provides a focused navigation through the most important interaction surfaces in a high-dimensional predictor space, allowing the analyst to inspect the key predictive mechanisms without the visual complexity of a full matrix display.

section: 13.3 Bayesian Additive Regression Trees and uncertainty-aware interpretability

13.3 Bayesian Additive Regression Trees and uncertainty-aware interpretability
Up to this point, most of the interpretability tools discussed in this chapter have been either model-dependent summaries for classical models or model-agnostic summaries applied to flexible predictive algorithms. This strategy is useful because it allows a common interpretive language across very different model classes. However, one important advantage of Bayesian machine learning models is that they do not provide only point predictions or point summaries of importance. Instead, they provide posterior distributions over predictive structures.
This motivates a final shift in the chapter. Rather than asking only which variables are important, how predictions vary across the predictor space, or how interactions appear on average, we now ask how stable these patterns are under posterior uncertainty. Bayesian Additive Regression Trees (BART) are especially useful in this setting because they represent the fitted function as a sum of many small trees while retaining a full posterior distribution over the model.
In the present example, BART achieved the best predictive performance among all fitted models. This makes it a natural model with which to conclude the chapter, since it allows us to move from interpretability as point summary toward interpretability as structured uncertainty assessment. To explore this idea, we now turn to structural summaries derived from the fitted BART model using the bartMan framework.

13.3.1 Why BART is different
Bayesian Additive Regression Trees model the regression function as a sum of weak trees,
\[
f(\mathbf{x}) = \sum_{j=1}^{m} g(\mathbf{x}; T_j, M_j),
\]
where each \(T_j\) denotes a tree structure and \(M_j\) its associated terminal-node parameters. In the Bayesian formulation, priors are placed over trees and terminal node values, and inference proceeds through posterior sampling. As a result, the fitted model is not a single deterministic function but a posterior distribution over functions.
This has an important interpretive consequence. Many familiar machine-learning summaries, such as variable importance or partial dependence, are often presented as fixed point estimates. In BART, however, these quantities may be examined across posterior draws, allowing the analyst to distinguish large effects from stable effects and to evaluate how uncertain a given structural pattern may be.

13.3.1.1 Fitting a Bayesian Additive Regression Trees model
In the previous sections of this chapter we examined several supervised learning algorithms and explored a variety of interpretability techniques, including coefficient analysis, tree structures, variable importance summaries, interaction matrices, and functional response plots such as partial dependence and ICE curves. We now turn to Bayesian Additive Regression Trees (BART), a model that combines the flexibility of tree ensembles with the uncertainty quantification provided by Bayesian inference.
Unlike many machine-learning algorithms that produce a single fitted model, BART represents the regression function as a posterior distribution over functions. Each posterior draw corresponds to one possible ensemble of trees consistent with the observed data. As a consequence, interpretability can be based not only on the central predictive function but also on the distribution of plausible models supported by the posterior.
In the following analysis we fit a BART model using the dbarts implementation. The fitted model produces posterior samples of predicted outcomes, posterior samples of the residual variance, and internal summaries describing how often predictors are used within the ensemble of trees. These components form the basis of an uncertainty-aware interpretability analysis.
The next chunk fits the BART model using the training data.

# ===============================================================
# Load fitted BART model and associated objects
# ===============================================================

bart_obj <- readRDS(file.path(models_dir, "bart_reg_small.rds"))

bart_fit <- bart_obj$model
X_train <- bart_obj$X_train
X_test  <- bart_obj$X_test
y_train <- bart_obj$y_train
y_test  <- bart_obj$y_test
predictor_names <- bart_obj$predictor_names


# ===============================================================
# Fit BART model
# ===============================================================

library(dbarts)
library(tidyverse)

set.seed(2026)

bart_fit <- dbarts::bart(
  x.train = X_train,
  y.train = y_train,
  x.test  = X_test,
  ntree   = 80,
  nskip   = 200,
  ndpost  = 600,
  keeptrees = TRUE,
  verbose = FALSE
)




13.3.2 Posterior predictions and predictive uncertainty
A central advantage of BART is that predictions are not represented by a single fitted value. Instead, the model produces posterior samples of predictions for each observation. This allows the analyst to examine not only the central prediction but also the uncertainty associated with that prediction.
In the fitted dbarts object, posterior predictive samples for the test set are stored in the matrix yhat.test. Each column corresponds to an observation and each row corresponds to a posterior draw. The vector yhat.test.mean contains the posterior mean prediction for each observation.
Because the posterior predictive distribution is available explicitly, credible intervals for predicted outcomes can be computed directly. These intervals summarize the range of predicted values supported by the posterior distribution and therefore provide a natural measure of predictive uncertainty.

# ===============================================================
# Posterior predictions
# ===============================================================

bart_pred_tbl <- tibble(
  obs_id   = seq_along(y_test),
  observed = y_test,
  pred_mean = bart_fit$yhat.test.mean,
  pred_q025 = apply(bart_fit$yhat.test, 2, quantile, 0.025),
  pred_q50  = apply(bart_fit$yhat.test, 2, quantile, 0.50),
  pred_q975 = apply(bart_fit$yhat.test, 2, quantile, 0.975)
)

bart_pred_tbl %>% slice_head(n = 10)

# A tibble: 10 × 6
   obs_id observed pred_mean pred_q025 pred_q50 pred_q975
    <int>    <dbl>     <dbl>     <dbl>    <dbl>     <dbl>
 1      1      133     216.   184.        217.      245. 
 2      2       67     129.    86.9       130.      168. 
 3      3      108     125.    86.1       126.      162. 
 4      4      212     200.   144.        200.      262. 
 5      5       30      51.5   16.6        50.8      89.5
 6      6      197     190.   152.        190.      224. 
 7      7       30      26.2   -7.25       25.9      59.6
 8      8       30      56.1   21.7        55.7      90.7
 9      9       30      24.1  -24.3        25.2      67.8
10     10       30      45.5   -0.0179     45.3      92.5



# ===============================================================
# Observed vs predicted with credible intervals
# ===============================================================

bart_pred_tbl %>%
  ggplot(aes(x = observed, y = pred_mean)) +
  geom_errorbar(aes(ymin = pred_q025, ymax = pred_q975), alpha = 0.35) +
  geom_point(size = 2) +
  geom_abline(intercept = 0, slope = 1, linetype = 2) +
  labs(
    title = "BART posterior predictions with 95% credible intervals",
    x = "Observed outcome",
    y = "Posterior mean prediction"
  ) +
  theme_bw(base_size = 12)









# ===============================================================
# Width of posterior predictive intervals
# ===============================================================

bart_pred_tbl <- bart_pred_tbl %>%
  mutate(ci_width = pred_q975 - pred_q025)

bart_pred_tbl %>%
  ggplot(aes(x = ci_width)) +
  geom_histogram(bins = 20) +
  labs(
    title = "Distribution of BART predictive interval widths",
    x = "Credible interval width",
    y = "Count"
  ) +
  theme_bw(base_size = 12)








The outputs presented in this section illustrate how the posterior predictive distribution produced by a BART model can be explored and interpreted in practice. Because BART generates many posterior draws of the regression function, each observation is associated not with a single predicted value but with a distribution of plausible predictions. The code above summarizes this information and produces three complementary outputs that help interpret the model’s predictive behavior and its associated uncertainty.
The first output is a small table showing the posterior predictive summaries for the first observations in the test set. For each observation, the table reports the observed outcome together with the posterior mean prediction and several quantiles of the posterior predictive distribution. The columns pred_q025 and pred_q975 define the bounds of the 95% credible interval, while pred_q50 corresponds to the posterior median. These summaries allow us to compare the observed values with the model’s central prediction and to inspect the range of outcomes that remain plausible under the posterior distribution.
The second output visualizes these predictions by plotting the observed outcome against the posterior mean prediction. Each point corresponds to one observation in the test set, and the vertical bars represent the 95% credible interval derived from the posterior predictive samples. The dashed diagonal line indicates perfect agreement between observed and predicted values. Points close to this line indicate accurate predictions, while the vertical bars illustrate the uncertainty associated with each prediction. In a Bayesian model such as BART, this uncertainty is an integral part of the predictive output rather than a separate post-hoc estimate.
The third output summarizes the width of the predictive credible intervals across all observations. By plotting the distribution of interval widths, we obtain a global view of how uncertain the model’s predictions are throughout the dataset. Narrow intervals correspond to observations for which the model produces stable predictions across posterior draws, while wider intervals indicate regions of the predictor space where predictions are more uncertain. Such variability in interval width often reflects differences in data density or complexity of the relationship between predictors and the outcome.


13.3.3 Variable usage across the posterior ensemble
Beyond predictive summaries, the BART model also provides structural information about how predictors are used within the posterior tree ensemble. In the dbarts object this information is stored in the matrix varcount. Each row corresponds to a posterior draw, and each column records how many times a predictor was used in tree splitting across the ensemble.
Although this measure does not represent a causal or marginal effect, it provides a useful structural summary of variable importance. Predictors that appear frequently and consistently across posterior draws can be interpreted as stable structural components of the ensemble.

# ===============================================================
# Variable usage across posterior draws
# ===============================================================

varcount_tbl <- as_tibble(bart_fit$varcount) %>%
  setNames(predictor_names) %>%
  mutate(draw = row_number()) %>%
  pivot_longer(
    cols = -draw,
    names_to = "term",
    values_to = "usage"
  )

var_usage_summary <- varcount_tbl %>%
  group_by(term) %>%
  summarise(
    mean_usage = mean(usage),
    sd_usage = sd(usage),
    .groups = "drop"
  ) %>%
  arrange(desc(mean_usage))

var_usage_summary

# A tibble: 5 × 3
  term     mean_usage sd_usage
  <chr>         <dbl>    <dbl>
1 wt.loss        25.4     4.10
2 ph.ecog        24.4     3.78
3 ph.karno       23.2     4.11
4 age            19.5     4.35
5 sex_male       18.6     3.73



# ===============================================================
# Posterior mean variable usage
# ===============================================================

var_usage_summary %>%
  ggplot(aes(x = reorder(term, mean_usage), y = mean_usage)) +
  geom_col() +
  coord_flip() +
  labs(
    title = "Posterior mean variable usage in BART",
    x = "",
    y = "Mean number of splits"
  ) +
  theme_bw(base_size = 12)










13.3.4 Structural interpretability with bartMan
While posterior predictions and variable usage provide useful summaries of predictive behavior, they do not yet reveal the internal structure of the tree ensemble. To examine these structural properties we use the bartMan framework, which extracts tree-level information from the fitted BART model and provides a set of visual tools for exploring the ensemble.
The first step is to extract the tree structures from the fitted BART object. This representation allows us to compute inclusion-based variable importance, interaction summaries, and tree-structure visualizations.
Internally, the dbarts implementation stores the posterior ensemble of trees in a compact format optimized for MCMC sampling and prediction. While efficient for computation, this internal representation is not immediately convenient for structural interpretation. The bartMan framework therefore provides a set of utilities that reorganize the fitted BART model into a tree-oriented structure designed for exploratory analysis.
The function extractTreeData() performs this transformation. It extracts the posterior trees from the fitted BART object and reconstructs them as an explicit collection of tree structures together with their associated split variables, node depths, and terminal node values. Importantly, this step does not refit the model. Instead, it simply translates the posterior tree ensemble into a format that allows downstream interpretability tools to operate on the structure of the ensemble.
The resulting object contains the full set of trees across posterior iterations and forms the basis for several interpretability diagnostics. Once the trees have been extracted, we can compute interaction matrices, visualize individual trees, examine splitting frequencies, and study structural patterns across the posterior ensemble.

bart_train_df <- as.data.frame(X_train)
colnames(bart_train_df) <- predictor_names
bart_train_df$y <- y_train


# ===============================================================
# Extract bartMan tree data
# ===============================================================
trees_data <- extractTreeData(
  model = bart_fit,
  data  = bart_train_df
)

saveRDS(
  trees_data,
  "/Users/danilosarti/Documents/ai_health_book/models/lung_sim_complete/bart_trees_data_small.rds"
)


trees_data<-readRDS(
  "/Users/danilosarti/Documents/ai_health_book/models/lung_sim_complete/bart_trees_data_small.rds"
)



13.3.5 VIVI interaction summaries for BART
Using the extracted tree structure we can compute VIVI matrices, which summarize variable importance and interaction strength jointly. In these matrices the diagonal elements represent marginal variable importance, while the off-diagonal elements represent pairwise interaction strength derived from the posterior tree ensemble.
The VIVI matrix provides a joint representation of variable importance and variable interaction strength derived directly from the posterior tree ensemble. Each element of the matrix summarizes how frequently variables appear within the splitting structure of the trees and how often they co-occur along decision paths.
In this representation, the diagonal elements correspond to marginal variable importance. These values reflect how often each predictor participates in splitting rules across the ensemble of posterior trees. Larger diagonal values therefore indicate predictors that play a central role in partitioning the predictor space.
The off-diagonal elements represent interaction strength between pairs of predictors. Interactions arise when two variables appear together along paths within the same trees, meaning that the effect of one predictor depends on the value of another. The magnitude of these entries summarizes how frequently such joint splitting patterns occur across the posterior ensemble.
The argument metric = "propMean" specifies that interaction strength is computed using the mean proportion of tree splits across posterior draws. This produces a stable summary of how strongly pairs of predictors participate in the structural decomposition of the response surface.
The resulting matrix therefore provides a structural view of the fitted model, revealing both which variables are influential and which combinations of variables jointly shape the predictive function.

# ===============================================================
# VIVI matrix
# ===============================================================

stdMat <- viviBartMatrix(
  trees = trees_data,
  type = "standard",
  metric = "propMean"
)

saveRDS(
  stdMat,
  "/Users/danilosarti/Documents/ai_health_book/models/lung_sim_complete/stdMat.rds"
)


library(bartMan)
viviBartPlot(stdMat)








The figure displays the VIVI matrix derived from the posterior tree ensemble of the BART model. This visualization jointly summarizes variable importance and pairwise interaction strength extracted from the splitting structure of the trees.
The diagonal elements of the matrix represent marginal variable importance (Vimp). These values measure how frequently each predictor appears in splitting rules across the ensemble of trees and across posterior draws. Variables with larger diagonal values therefore contribute more strongly to the partitioning of the predictor space. In the present model, the largest diagonal values are observed for wt.loss, ph.ecog, and ph.karno, indicating that these predictors play the most prominent role in shaping the predictive structure of the BART model. This result is consistent with earlier analyses in this chapter, where measures of patient functional status and clinical deterioration emerged as key determinants of predicted survival.
The off-diagonal elements represent pairwise interaction strength (Vint) between predictors. These entries quantify how frequently two variables appear together along decision paths within the trees. Larger values therefore indicate stronger structural interactions in the posterior ensemble. The strongest interaction in the matrix occurs between wt.loss and ph.ecog, suggesting that the model frequently uses these two predictors jointly when partitioning the predictor space. This indicates that the effect of weight loss on predicted survival depends strongly on the patient’s performance status.
A second notable interaction appears between wt.loss and ph.karno, again reflecting the close relationship between physical deterioration and functional capacity. Since the Karnofsky score and ECOG score both measure aspects of patient performance status, their interactions with weight loss are clinically plausible: the prognostic effect of weight loss is likely to differ depending on the patient’s overall functional condition.
By contrast, predictors such as sex_male and age show weaker interaction patterns. Their off-diagonal values are relatively small, indicating that these variables are used less frequently in joint splitting rules with other predictors. Although these variables still contribute to the predictive model, their influence appears to be more marginal compared with the functional status indicators.


13.3.6 Visualising the posterior tree ensemble
Although BART is an ensemble model, individual trees can still be inspected to understand how the predictor space is partitioned locally. The following plots show selected trees from the posterior ensemble.
Because BART represents the regression function as the sum of many small trees, the internal structure of the model can also be examined at the level of individual trees. Unlike classical decision trees such as CART, however, a single BART tree should not be interpreted as a standalone predictive model. Each tree typically contributes only a small component to the overall regression function, and the final prediction arises from the sum of many such weak learners.
Visualizing individual trees is therefore useful not for extracting deterministic decision rules, but for understanding how the ensemble partitions the predictor space locally. By inspecting the splitting variables and tree depths, one can observe how the model distributes predictive structure across multiple simple trees.
The plotSingleTree() function displays one tree from a specific posterior iteration. This provides a detailed view of the local splitting rules and the hierarchical structure of the partitions induced by that tree. Different visualization styles, such as dendrogram and icicle layouts, emphasize different aspects of the tree topology.
The plotTrees() function extends this idea by visualizing several trees from a given posterior iteration simultaneously. This allows the analyst to see how multiple trees contribute to the overall ensemble structure. Because BART models typically contain many shallow trees, these visualizations often reveal repeated splitting patterns involving a small number of influential predictors.

# ===============================================================
# Visualise individual trees
# ===============================================================

plotSingleTree(
  trees = trees_data,
  treeNo = 1,
  iter = 1,
  plotType = "dendrogram"
)

Iteration 1 and Tree Number 1 Selected.








plotSingleTree(
  trees = trees_data,
  treeNo = 1,
  iter = 1,
  plotType = "icicle"
)

Iteration 1 and Tree Number 1 Selected.









The figures above show two visual representations of a single tree extracted from the posterior BART ensemble. The first plot presents the tree in dendrogram form, which highlights the hierarchical sequence of splitting rules, while the second plot shows the same structure in an icicle representation, which emphasizes how the predictor space is partitioned into regions.
It is important to remember that in a BART model no individual tree represents the final predictive model. Unlike classical decision trees such as CART, where the entire predictive structure is contained in one tree, BART represents the regression function as the sum of many small trees. Each individual tree contributes only a small adjustment to the overall prediction. Consequently, the trees in a BART ensemble are typically shallow and simple, and their interpretation should be understood in the context of the ensemble rather than in isolation.
In the dendrogram representation, the root node shows the first partition of the predictor space, which in this case is based on weight loss (wt.loss). Observations with standardized weight loss below the threshold are sent to the left branch, while those above the threshold follow the right branch. The left branch is further partitioned using Karnofsky performance score (ph.karno), illustrating how the model refines predictions by combining multiple indicators of patient condition. The terminal nodes display small numeric values representing the contribution of that tree to the predicted outcome. These values are typically modest because the final prediction is obtained by summing contributions from many trees across the ensemble.
The icicle representation provides an alternative view of the same structure. Instead of focusing on hierarchical branching, the icicle plot emphasizes how the predictor space is divided into rectangular regions corresponding to the terminal nodes of the tree. Each block represents a region of the predictor space in which the model assigns the same local contribution to the prediction. The colors highlight these regions and help visualize how the tree partitions the space according to the splitting variables.
Taken together, these plots illustrate the local decision structure learned by one tree in the BART ensemble. Although each tree is simple, the aggregation of many such trees allows the model to approximate complex nonlinear relationships and interactions among predictors. Examining individual trees therefore provides insight into the basic building blocks of the model while reinforcing the idea that the predictive function emerges from the collective behavior of the entire ensemble.

plotTrees(
  trees = trees_data,
  iter = 1,
  removeStump = TRUE,
  selectedVars = c("age", "sex_male", "ph.ecog", "ph.karno", "wt.loss")
)

Iteration 1 Selected.









The figure above displays a collection of trees extracted from a single posterior iteration of the BART ensemble. Each small panel corresponds to one tree, and the colored regions indicate which predictor variable is used in the splitting rule at the root of that tree. The legend associates colors with the predictors: age, ph.ecog, ph.karno, sex_male, and wt.loss. The gray blocks represent terminal nodes where no further splitting occurs.
Several important structural properties of BART models become apparent in this visualization. First, the trees are small and shallow. Most trees contain only one or two splits before reaching terminal nodes. This is a characteristic design feature of BART: instead of fitting a few deep trees, the algorithm constructs a large ensemble of weak learners whose contributions are summed to approximate the regression function.
Second, the visualization highlights which predictors tend to appear near the root of the trees. Variables such as wt.loss, ph.ecog, and ph.karno appear frequently as root splitting variables across many trees. This pattern reinforces the importance results observed earlier in the VIVI matrix, where these variables also exhibited strong marginal importance and interaction structure. Their repeated appearance at the top of the trees indicates that the model often begins its partitioning of the predictor space using indicators related to patient functional status and clinical deterioration.
By contrast, variables such as age and sex_male appear less frequently as primary splitting variables. When they do appear, they typically contribute secondary refinements within the partitioning structure rather than defining the main divisions of the predictor space. This suggests that demographic variables play a more modest role in the predictive structure compared with clinical status indicators.
Finally, the figure illustrates how the BART model distributes predictive complexity across many small trees rather than concentrating it in a single structure. Each tree contributes a small local adjustment to the overall regression function. When hundreds of such trees are aggregated across posterior draws, the ensemble is able to approximate complex nonlinear relationships and interaction effects while maintaining relatively simple individual components.


13.3.7 VSUPS
While the standard VIVI matrix summarizes the average importance and interaction strength across the posterior ensemble, it does not explicitly represent the stability of these structural patterns. Two variable interactions may have similar average magnitudes but very different levels of variability across posterior draws.
To address this limitation, the bartMan framework provides the VSUP (Variable Selection Uncertainty Plot) representation. VSUP extends the VIVI matrix by incorporating a measure of uncertainty associated with each importance and interaction estimate. This allows the analyst to distinguish interactions that are consistently present across posterior draws from those that appear only sporadically.
In the code below, the VSUP matrix is computed using the argument type = "vsup". The option metricError = "CV" specifies that uncertainty is quantified using the coefficient of variation across posterior draws. Interactions with higher variability therefore appear with stronger uncertainty signals in the visualization.
The resulting plot encodes two dimensions simultaneously: the magnitude of importance or interaction and the stability of that quantity across the posterior distribution. This representation highlights structural relationships that are both strong and stable, providing an uncertainty-aware perspective on the internal structure of the BART model.

vsupMat <- viviBartMatrix(
  trees = trees_data,
  type = "vsup",
  metric = "propMean",
  metricError = "CV"
)

saveRDS(
  vsupMat,
  file.path(models_dir, "vsupMat.rds")
)


viviBartPlot(
  vsupMat,
  max_desat = 1,
  pow_desat = 0.6,
  max_light = 0.6,
  pow_light = 1,
  label = "CV"
)








The figure above displays the VSUP (Variable Selection Uncertainty Plot) matrix derived from the posterior BART ensemble. This visualization extends the standard VIVI matrix by simultaneously representing variable importance, interaction strength, and the stability of these quantities across posterior draws.
As in the standard VIVI matrix, the diagonal elements represent marginal variable importance (Vimp). These values summarize how frequently each predictor appears in the splitting rules of the posterior tree ensemble. In this model, the diagonal entries indicate that wt.loss and ph.ecog remain among the most influential predictors, followed by ph.karno, while age and sex_male contribute more modestly to the predictive structure. This ranking is consistent with earlier results showing that variables related to patient functional status dominate the predictive architecture.
The off-diagonal elements represent pairwise interaction strength (Vint), indicating how often two predictors appear together along splitting paths in the ensemble of trees. The strongest interaction again appears between ph.ecog and wt.loss, confirming that the model frequently combines these variables when partitioning the predictor space. This interaction is clinically plausible, as weight loss and performance status often jointly reflect disease severity and physiological decline.
The distinctive feature of the VSUP representation is that it also encodes the uncertainty of these structural summaries. The circular scales shown on the right indicate how variability across posterior draws is represented through the coefficient of variation (CV). In this framework, interactions or importance measures that remain stable across posterior samples appear with stronger and more saturated colors, while relationships with greater variability appear more muted. This allows the analyst to distinguish structural patterns that are consistently supported by the posterior from those that fluctuate more substantially across draws.
In the present model, the strong interaction between ph.ecog and wt.loss not only has high magnitude but also appears relatively stable across posterior samples, reinforcing the conclusion that these variables jointly define an important region of the predictor space. By contrast, weaker interactions involving age or sex_male display lower magnitude and greater variability, suggesting that their influence is less central to the ensemble’s predictive structure.

text:
13.4 Appendix

# ===============================================================
# 01_train_models_lung_sim_complete.R
# Interpretable AI — unified training script using lung_sim_complete
# ---------------------------------------------------------------
# Models:
# - OLS
# - LASSO / Ridge / Elastic Net
# - Regression Tree
# - Random Forest (ranger)
# - XGBoost
# - BART (dbarts)
# ---------------------------------------------------------------
# Design choices:
# - complete dataset (no missingness)
# - 5 clinical predictors only
# - continuous outcome: time
# - auxiliary binary outcome: status_bin (excluded from predictors)
# - save train/test/preprocessing objects for interpretability workflows
# ===============================================================

# ----------------------------
# 0) Packages
# ----------------------------
pkgs <- c(
  "tidyverse", "tidymodels", "glmnet",
  "rpart", "ranger", "xgboost",
  "dbarts", "broom"
)

to_install <- pkgs[!pkgs %in% rownames(installed.packages())]
if (length(to_install) > 0) install.packages(to_install)

suppressPackageStartupMessages({
  library(tidyverse)
  library(tidymodels)
  library(glmnet)
  library(rpart)
  library(ranger)
  library(xgboost)
  library(dbarts)
  library(broom)
})

# ----------------------------
# 1) Paths + read data
# ----------------------------
data_path  <- "/Users/danilosarti/Documents/ai_health_book/data/lung_sim_complete.rds"
models_dir <- "/Users/danilosarti/Documents/ai_health_book/models/lung_sim_complete"
dir.create(models_dir, recursive = TRUE, showWarnings = FALSE)

df_small <- readRDS(data_path)

# ----------------------------
# 2) Targets / ID
# ----------------------------
y_cont <- "time"
y_bin  <- "status_bin"
id_col <- "patient_id"

# ----------------------------
# 3) Split data
# ----------------------------
set.seed(2026)

spl <- initial_split(df_small, prop = 0.75, strata = status_bin)
train_df <- training(spl)
test_df  <- testing(spl)

# ----------------------------
# 4) Preprocessing recipe
# ---------------------------------------------------------------
# Keep:
# - raw train/test data
# - baked train/test data
# - status_bin removed from predictors to avoid leakage
# ---------------------------------------------------------------
rec_base <- recipe(
  formula(paste(y_cont, "~ .")),
  data = train_df
) %>%
  update_role(all_of(id_col), new_role = "id") %>%
  step_rm(all_of(c(id_col, y_bin, "status"))) %>%
  step_dummy(all_nominal_predictors(), one_hot = FALSE) %>%
  step_zv(all_predictors()) %>%
  step_normalize(all_numeric_predictors())

prep_rec <- prep(rec_base, training = train_df, verbose = FALSE)

train_baked <- bake(prep_rec, new_data = train_df)
test_baked  <- bake(prep_rec, new_data = test_df)

X_train <- train_baked %>% select(-all_of(y_cont)) %>% as.matrix()
X_test  <- test_baked  %>% select(-all_of(y_cont)) %>% as.matrix()

y_train <- train_baked[[y_cont]]
y_test  <- test_baked[[y_cont]]

predictor_names <- colnames(X_train)

# ----------------------------
# 5) Save preprocessing objects
# ----------------------------
saveRDS(
  list(
    split = spl,
    recipe = prep_rec,
    train_df = train_df,
    test_df = test_df,
    train_baked = train_baked,
    test_baked = test_baked,
    X_train = X_train,
    X_test = X_test,
    y_train = y_train,
    y_test = y_test,
    predictor_names = predictor_names,
    y_cont = y_cont,
    y_bin = y_bin,
    id_col = id_col
  ),
  file = file.path(models_dir, "prep_objects.rds")
)

# ----------------------------
# 6) Helper metrics
# ----------------------------
rmse_vec <- yardstick::rmse_vec
mae_vec  <- yardstick::mae_vec

# ===============================================================
# 7) OLS
# ===============================================================
ols_fit <- lm(time ~ ., data = train_baked)
ols_pred <- predict(ols_fit, newdata = test_baked)

ols_metrics <- tibble(
  model = "OLS",
  rmse = rmse_vec(y_test, ols_pred),
  mae  = mae_vec(y_test, ols_pred)
)

coef_ols_tbl <- broom::tidy(ols_fit) %>%
  transmute(
    model = "OLS",
    term = term,
    estimate = estimate,
    std.error = std.error,
    statistic = statistic,
    p.value = p.value
  ) %>%
  filter(term != "(Intercept)") %>%
  mutate(abs_estimate = abs(estimate))

saveRDS(
  list(
    model = ols_fit,
    metrics = ols_metrics,
    coef_tbl = coef_ols_tbl
  ),
  file = file.path(models_dir, "ols_small.rds")
)

# ===============================================================
# 8) Regularized regression: LASSO / Ridge / Elastic Net
# ===============================================================
set.seed(2026)

fit_glmnet_cv <- function(X, y, alpha, family = "gaussian", nfolds = 10) {
  cv.glmnet(
    x = X,
    y = y,
    family = family,
    alpha = alpha,
    nfolds = nfolds,
    standardize = FALSE
  )
}

lasso_cv <- fit_glmnet_cv(X_train, y_train, alpha = 1)
ridge_cv <- fit_glmnet_cv(X_train, y_train, alpha = 0)

enet_alpha <- 0.5
enet_cv <- fit_glmnet_cv(X_train, y_train, alpha = enet_alpha)

mod_lasso <- glmnet(
  X_train, y_train,
  alpha = 1,
  lambda = lasso_cv$lambda.min,
  standardize = FALSE
)

mod_ridge <- glmnet(
  X_train, y_train,
  alpha = 0,
  lambda = ridge_cv$lambda.min,
  standardize = FALSE
)

mod_enet <- glmnet(
  X_train, y_train,
  alpha = enet_alpha,
  lambda = enet_cv$lambda.min,
  standardize = FALSE
)

pred_lasso <- as.numeric(predict(mod_lasso, newx = X_test))
pred_ridge <- as.numeric(predict(mod_ridge, newx = X_test))
pred_enet  <- as.numeric(predict(mod_enet,  newx = X_test))

glmnet_metrics <- bind_rows(
  tibble(model = "LASSO", rmse = rmse_vec(y_test, pred_lasso), mae = mae_vec(y_test, pred_lasso)),
  tibble(model = "Ridge", rmse = rmse_vec(y_test, pred_ridge), mae = mae_vec(y_test, pred_ridge)),
  tibble(model = paste0("ElasticNet_a", enet_alpha), rmse = rmse_vec(y_test, pred_enet), mae = mae_vec(y_test, pred_enet))
)

coef_lasso_tbl <- as.matrix(coef(mod_lasso)) %>%
  as.data.frame() %>%
  tibble::rownames_to_column("term") %>%
  rename(estimate = s0) %>%
  mutate(
    model = "LASSO",
    std.error = NA_real_,
    statistic = NA_real_,
    p.value = NA_real_
  ) %>%
  filter(term != "(Intercept)") %>%
  mutate(abs_estimate = abs(estimate))

coef_ridge_tbl <- as.matrix(coef(mod_ridge)) %>%
  as.data.frame() %>%
  tibble::rownames_to_column("term") %>%
  rename(estimate = s0) %>%
  mutate(
    model = "Ridge",
    std.error = NA_real_,
    statistic = NA_real_,
    p.value = NA_real_
  ) %>%
  filter(term != "(Intercept)") %>%
  mutate(abs_estimate = abs(estimate))

coef_enet_tbl <- as.matrix(coef(mod_enet)) %>%
  as.data.frame() %>%
  tibble::rownames_to_column("term") %>%
  rename(estimate = s0) %>%
  mutate(
    model = paste0("ElasticNet_a", enet_alpha),
    std.error = NA_real_,
    statistic = NA_real_,
    p.value = NA_real_
  ) %>%
  filter(term != "(Intercept)") %>%
  mutate(abs_estimate = abs(estimate))

coef_all_tbl <- bind_rows(
  coef_ols_tbl,
  coef_lasso_tbl,
  coef_ridge_tbl,
  coef_enet_tbl
)

coef_sparsity_tbl <- bind_rows(
  coef_lasso_tbl %>%
    summarise(
      model = "LASSO",
      n_nonzero = sum(estimate != 0),
      n_zero = sum(estimate == 0)
    ),
  coef_ridge_tbl %>%
    summarise(
      model = "Ridge",
      n_nonzero = sum(estimate != 0),
      n_zero = sum(estimate == 0)
    ),
  coef_enet_tbl %>%
    summarise(
      model = paste0("ElasticNet_a", enet_alpha),
      n_nonzero = sum(estimate != 0),
      n_zero = sum(estimate == 0)
    )
)

saveRDS(
  list(
    lasso = lasso_cv,
    ridge = ridge_cv,
    enet = enet_cv,
    mod_lasso = mod_lasso,
    mod_ridge = mod_ridge,
    mod_enet = mod_enet,
    enet_alpha = enet_alpha,
    metrics = glmnet_metrics,
    coef_lasso_tbl = coef_lasso_tbl,
    coef_ridge_tbl = coef_ridge_tbl,
    coef_enet_tbl = coef_enet_tbl,
    coef_all_tbl = coef_all_tbl,
    coef_sparsity_tbl = coef_sparsity_tbl
  ),
  file = file.path(models_dir, "glmnet_small.rds")
)

# ===============================================================
# 9) Regression tree (rpart)
# ===============================================================
set.seed(2026)

tree_fit <- rpart::rpart(
  time ~ .,
  data = train_baked,
  method = "anova",
  control = rpart::rpart.control(cp = 0.001, maxdepth = 5, minsplit = 15)
)

cp_tbl <- tree_fit$cptable
best_row <- which.min(cp_tbl[, "xerror"])
best_cp  <- cp_tbl[best_row, "CP"]

tree_pruned <- rpart::prune(tree_fit, cp = best_cp)
tree_pred <- predict(tree_pruned, newdata = test_baked)

tree_metrics <- tibble(
  model = "Tree_rpart",
  rmse = rmse_vec(y_test, tree_pred),
  mae  = mae_vec(y_test, tree_pred)
)

saveRDS(
  list(
    model = tree_pruned,
    metrics = tree_metrics,
    cp_table = cp_tbl,
    best_cp = best_cp
  ),
  file = file.path(models_dir, "tree_reg_small.rds")
)

# ===============================================================
# 10) Random Forest (ranger)
# ===============================================================
set.seed(2026)

rf_fit <- ranger(
  formula = time ~ .,
  data = train_baked,
  num.trees = 500,
  mtry = max(1, floor(sqrt(ncol(train_baked) - 1))),
  min.node.size = 8,
  importance = "impurity",
  seed = 2026
)

rf_pred <- predict(rf_fit, data = test_baked)$predictions

rf_metrics <- tibble(
  model = "RF_ranger",
  rmse = rmse_vec(y_test, rf_pred),
  mae  = mae_vec(y_test, rf_pred)
)

saveRDS(
  list(
    model = rf_fit,
    metrics = rf_metrics,
    vimp = rf_fit$variable.importance,
    importance_type = "impurity"
  ),
  file = file.path(models_dir, "rf_reg_small.rds")
)

# ===============================================================
# 11) XGBoost regression
# ===============================================================
set.seed(2026)

dtrain <- xgb.DMatrix(data = X_train, label = y_train)
dtest  <- xgb.DMatrix(data = X_test,  label = y_test)

params <- list(
  objective = "reg:squarederror",
  eval_metric = "rmse",
  eta = 0.03,
  max_depth = 3,
  min_child_weight = 3,
  subsample = 0.8,
  colsample_bytree = 0.8
)

xgb_fit <- xgb.train(
  params = params,
  data = dtrain,
  nrounds = 800,
  watchlist = list(train = dtrain, test = dtest),
  early_stopping_rounds = 30,
  verbose = 0
)

xgb_pred <- predict(xgb_fit, dtest)

xgb_metrics <- tibble(
  model = "XGB_reg",
  rmse = rmse_vec(y_test, xgb_pred),
  mae  = mae_vec(y_test, xgb_pred)
)

xgb_imp <- xgb.importance(model = xgb_fit)

saveRDS(
  list(
    model = xgb_fit,
    metrics = xgb_metrics,
    importance = xgb_imp,
    params = params,
    feature_names = predictor_names
  ),
  file = file.path(models_dir, "xgb_reg_small.rds")
)

# ===============================================================
# 12) BART regression (dbarts)
# ===============================================================
set.seed(2026)

bart_fit <- dbarts::bart(
  x.train = X_train,
  y.train = y_train,
  x.test  = X_test,
  keeptrees = TRUE,
  ntree = 80,
  nskip = 200,
  ndpost = 600,
  verbose = FALSE
)

bart_pred_mean <- colMeans(bart_fit$yhat.test)

bart_metrics <- tibble(
  model = "BART_dbarts",
  rmse = rmse_vec(y_test, bart_pred_mean),
  mae  = mae_vec(y_test, bart_pred_mean)
)

saveRDS(
  list(
    model = bart_fit,
    metrics = bart_metrics,
    X_train = X_train,
    X_test = X_test,
    y_train = y_train,
    y_test = y_test,
    predictor_names = predictor_names
  ),
  file = file.path(models_dir, "bart_reg_small.rds")
)

# ===============================================================
# 13) Save combined continuous-model metrics
# ===============================================================
metrics_tbl <- bind_rows(
  ols_metrics,
  glmnet_metrics,
  tree_metrics,
  rf_metrics,
  xgb_metrics,
  bart_metrics
) %>%
  arrange(rmse)

print(metrics_tbl)

saveRDS(
  metrics_tbl,
  file = file.path(models_dir, "metrics_comparison_continuous_no_nn.rds")
)

# ===============================================================
# End main training script
# ===============================================================


# ===============================================================
# CHUNK 2 — Neural Network training (robust Keras 3 version)
# ===============================================================
# What this chunk does:
# - Reads the SAME baked train/test data used in the chapter
# - Builds a small feed-forward neural network for regression
# - Converts R objects explicitly to NumPy float32 arrays
# - Trains the model safely under Keras 3 + reticulate
# - Evaluates RMSE and MAE on the test set
# - Saves the trained model in .keras format
# - Saves a companion .rds object with metrics + history_df + model path
# - Reloads the saved model as a sanity check
# ===============================================================

library(keras)
library(reticulate)
library(tidyverse)
library(yardstick)

# ---------------------------------------------------------------
# 1) Ensure the correct Python environment is used
# ---------------------------------------------------------------
use_virtualenv(
  "/Users/danilosarti/Documents/ai_health_book/.venv-genai",
  required = TRUE
)

# Optional diagnostics
print(py_config())
print(py_module_available("tensorflow"))
print(py_module_available("keras"))
print(py_module_available("numpy"))

# ---------------------------------------------------------------
# 2) Paths
# ---------------------------------------------------------------
models_dir <- "/Users/danilosarti/Documents/ai_health_book/models/lung_sim_complete"

# ---------------------------------------------------------------
# 3) Read preprocessing objects
# ---------------------------------------------------------------
prep_obj <- readRDS(file.path(models_dir, "prep_objects.rds"))

train_baked <- prep_obj$train_baked
test_baked  <- prep_obj$test_baked
y_cont      <- prep_obj$y_cont

# ---------------------------------------------------------------
# 4) Prepare matrices
# ---------------------------------------------------------------
X_train <- train_baked %>%
  dplyr::select(-all_of(y_cont)) %>%
  as.data.frame() %>%
  data.matrix()

X_test <- test_baked %>%
  dplyr::select(-all_of(y_cont)) %>%
  as.data.frame() %>%
  data.matrix()

y_train <- as.numeric(train_baked[[y_cont]])
y_test  <- as.numeric(test_baked[[y_cont]])

# Force storage mode explicitly
storage.mode(X_train) <- "double"
storage.mode(X_test)  <- "double"
storage.mode(y_train) <- "double"
storage.mode(y_test)  <- "double"

# Safety checks
stopifnot(is.matrix(X_train))
stopifnot(is.matrix(X_test))
stopifnot(is.numeric(y_train))
stopifnot(is.numeric(y_test))
stopifnot(!anyNA(X_train))
stopifnot(!anyNA(X_test))
stopifnot(!anyNA(y_train))
stopifnot(!anyNA(y_test))
stopifnot(all(is.finite(X_train)))
stopifnot(all(is.finite(X_test)))
stopifnot(all(is.finite(y_train)))
stopifnot(all(is.finite(y_test)))

cat("X_train dim:", dim(X_train), "\n")
cat("X_test dim:", dim(X_test), "\n")
cat("y_train length:", length(y_train), "\n")
cat("y_test length:", length(y_test), "\n")

# ---------------------------------------------------------------
# 5) Convert explicitly to NumPy float32 arrays
# ---------------------------------------------------------------
np <- import("numpy", convert = FALSE)

X_train_np <- np$array(X_train, dtype = "float32")
X_test_np  <- np$array(X_test, dtype = "float32")

# For regression, pass y as column vector
y_train_np <- np$array(matrix(y_train, ncol = 1), dtype = "float32")
y_test_np  <- np$array(matrix(y_test,  ncol = 1), dtype = "float32")

# ---------------------------------------------------------------
# 6) Build neural network
# ---------------------------------------------------------------
set.seed(2026)

inputs <- layer_input(
  shape = c(ncol(X_train)),
  name = "input"
)

outputs <- inputs %>%
  layer_dense(units = 64, activation = "relu", name = "dense_1") %>%
  layer_dropout(rate = 0.15, name = "dropout_1") %>%
  layer_dense(units = 32, activation = "relu", name = "dense_2") %>%
  layer_dropout(rate = 0.15, name = "dropout_2") %>%
  layer_dense(units = 1, activation = "linear", name = "output")

nn_model <- keras_model(
  inputs = inputs,
  outputs = outputs,
  name = "nn_reg"
)

# ---------------------------------------------------------------
# 7) Compile model
# ---------------------------------------------------------------
nn_model$compile(
  optimizer = optimizer_adam(learning_rate = 1e-3),
  loss = "mse",
  metrics = list("mae")
)

# ---------------------------------------------------------------
# 8) Train model
# ---------------------------------------------------------------
history <- nn_model$fit(
  x = X_train_np,
  y = y_train_np,
  validation_split = 0.2,
  epochs = as.integer(200),
  batch_size = as.integer(16),
  callbacks = list(
    callback_early_stopping(
      patience = as.integer(20),
      restore_best_weights = TRUE
    )
  ),
  verbose = as.integer(1)
)

# ---------------------------------------------------------------
# 9) Predict on test set
# ---------------------------------------------------------------
nn_pred <- as.numeric(nn_model$predict(X_test_np))

# ---------------------------------------------------------------
# 10) Compute metrics
# ---------------------------------------------------------------
nn_metrics <- tibble(
  model = "NN_reg",
  rmse = yardstick::rmse_vec(y_test, nn_pred),
  mae  = yardstick::mae_vec(y_test, nn_pred)
)

print(nn_metrics)

# ---------------------------------------------------------------
# 11) Save neural network
# ---------------------------------------------------------------
nn_model_path <- file.path(models_dir, "nn_reg_small.keras")
nn_model$save(filepath = nn_model_path)

# ---------------------------------------------------------------
# 12) Extract training history safely
# ---------------------------------------------------------------
history_df <- NULL
hist_list <- NULL

if (!is.null(history$history)) {
  hist_list <- history$history
}

if (!is.null(hist_list)) {
  metric_names <- names(hist_list)

  if (length(metric_names) > 0) {
    n_epochs <- length(as.numeric(unlist(hist_list[[1]])))
    history_df <- tibble(epoch = seq_len(n_epochs))

    for (nm in metric_names) {
      history_df[[nm]] <- as.numeric(unlist(hist_list[[nm]]))
    }
  }
}

print(history_df)

# ---------------------------------------------------------------
# 13) Save companion object
# ---------------------------------------------------------------
saveRDS(
  list(
    metrics = nn_metrics,
    history_df = history_df,
    model_path = nn_model_path
  ),
  file = file.path(models_dir, "nn_reg_small_history.rds")
)

# ---------------------------------------------------------------
# 14) Sanity check: reload saved model
# ---------------------------------------------------------------
nn_model_reload <- keras::load_model_tf(nn_model_path)

nn_pred_reload <- as.numeric(nn_model_reload$predict(X_test_np))

reload_check <- tibble(
  original = nn_pred,
  reloaded = nn_pred_reload,
  abs_diff = abs(nn_pred - nn_pred_reload)
)

print(summary(reload_check$abs_diff))

# ---------------------------------------------------------------
# End chunk
# ---------------------------------------------------------------


# ===============================================================
# 03_collect_metrics_lung_sim_complete.R
# Collect all final model performance metrics
# ===============================================================

library(tidyverse)

models_dir <- "/Users/danilosarti/Documents/ai_health_book/models/lung_sim_complete"

ols_obj    <- readRDS(file.path(models_dir, "ols_small.rds"))
glmnet_obj <- readRDS(file.path(models_dir, "glmnet_small.rds"))
tree_obj   <- readRDS(file.path(models_dir, "tree_reg_small.rds"))
rf_obj     <- readRDS(file.path(models_dir, "rf_reg_small.rds"))
xgb_obj    <- readRDS(file.path(models_dir, "xgb_reg_small.rds"))
bart_obj   <- readRDS(file.path(models_dir, "bart_reg_small.rds"))
nn_obj     <- readRDS(file.path(models_dir, "nn_reg_small_history.rds"))

metrics_tbl <- bind_rows(
  ols_obj$metrics,
  glmnet_obj$metrics,
  tree_obj$metrics,
  rf_obj$metrics,
  xgb_obj$metrics,
  bart_obj$metrics,
  nn_obj$metrics
) %>%
  arrange(rmse)

print(metrics_tbl)

saveRDS(
  metrics_tbl,
  file = file.path(models_dir, "metrics_comparison_continuous.rds")
)

title: 10  Gen_AI Foundations I: Language as Computation
text:
10.1 Language and computation
Human beings interact with language long before they formalize it. We intuitively understand that language is layered: it carries symbols, structure, meaning, intention, and context. We speak of natural language (English, Portuguese, Chinese), mathematical language (equations and formal notation), and programming languages (R, Python, C++). Although these systems differ in purpose and structure, they share a central property: they encode information through structured symbols governed by rules.
Computers, however, do not process symbols directly. They process numbers. More precisely, they process binary numbers—sequences of bits (0s and 1s). Every operation performed by a computer ultimately reduces to numerical manipulation in binary form. Text, images, audio, and even entire databases are stored and transformed as numerical patterns in memory.
This leads to a crucial conceptual shift: before a computer can work with language, language must be converted into numbers.
When we interact with computers, text is first represented as strings—ordered sequences of characters. A sentence such as:
“The patient reports pain”
is not stored as meaning. It is stored as a sequence of symbols encoded numerically according to a character encoding standard, typically Unicode (most commonly UTF-8 in modern systems).
Behind the scenes, each character is mapped to an integer code point. That integer is then stored in binary form in memory. For example:
The two outputs above illustrate different layers of numerical representation.
The function utf8ToInt() converts each character in the sentence into its Unicode integer code. For example, the character T is represented by the integer 84, while the space character corresponds to 32. This step shows how textual symbols are mapped to numeric identifiers.
The function intToBits() then reveals how these integers are stored in computer memory. Each integer is represented internally as a sequence of binary digits. For instance, the number 84 corresponds to the binary pattern 01010100.
Conceptually, this demonstrates a fundamental property of computational systems: all textual information is ultimately represented as binary data. However, machine learning models rarely operate directly on these raw bit patterns. Instead, higher-level representations such as tokens, token identifiers, and embeddings are used to structure linguistic information in a form suitable for statistical learning. Those bits are what the computer actually manipulates.
So at the lowest level, language inside a computer is nothing more than structured binary data.
This reveals an important abstraction chain:
Meaning (human level) → Symbols (words, characters) → Integers (Unicode code points) → Binary bits (machine level)
Meaning does not exist inside the machine. It must be constructed through computation over numerical representations. The string representation is therefore the first abstraction layer—human language converted into structured symbolic data, and then into numbers.
The following codes illustrate the ideas previously discussed.
# A simple sentence stored as a string
sentence <- "The patient reports pain"

sentence

[1] "The patient reports pain"

class(sentence)

[1] "character"
In R, this object is of type “character”, but internally it is stored as encoded numerical data.
# Split into individual characters
chars <- strsplit(sentence, "")[[1]]

chars

 [1] "T" "h" "e" " " "p" "a" "t" "i" "e" "n" "t" " " "r" "e" "p" "o" "r" "t" "s"
[20] " " "p" "a" "i" "n"

length(chars)

[1] 24
The sentence is now an ordered sequence of discrete symbols.
# Convert characters to their UTF-8 integer representation
char_codes <- utf8ToInt(sentence)

char_codes

 [1]  84 104 101  32 112  97 116 105 101 110 116  32 114 101 112 111 114 116 115
[20]  32 112  97 105 110
Now we see the numerical layer: each character has become an integer.
# Show binary representation of first few characters
intToBits(char_codes[1])

 [1] 00 00 01 00 01 00 01 00 00 00 00 00 00 00 00 00 00 00 00 00 00 00 00 00 00
[26] 00 00 00 00 00 00 00
And here we reach the lowest level: binary bits. This is what the hardware ultimately processes.
The two outputs above illustrate different layers of numerical representation. The function utf8ToInt() converts each character in the sentence into its Unicode integer code. For example, the character T is represented by the integer 84, while the space character corresponds to 32. This step shows how textual symbols are mapped to numeric identifiers.
The function intToBits() then reveals how these integers are stored in computer memory. Each integer is represented internally as a sequence of binary digits. For instance, the number 84 corresponds to the binary pattern 01010100.
tibble(
  character = str_split(sentence, "")[[1]],
  unicode = utf8ToInt(sentence),
  binary = sapply(utf8ToInt(sentence), function(x) {
    paste(rev(intToBits(x)[1:8]), collapse = "")
  })
)

# A tibble: 24 × 3
   character unicode binary          
   <chr>       <int> <chr>           
 1 "T"            84 0001000100010000
 2 "h"           104 0001010001000000

Once language is stored as structured symbolic sequences, computational operations become possible. We can measure length, search for patterns, extract substrings, compare sequences, and transform characters. The following codes implement examples of such operations:
# String length
nchar(sentence)

[1] 24

# Detect pattern
grepl("pain", sentence)

[1] TRUE

# Replace text
gsub("pain", "discomfort", sentence)

[1] "The patient reports discomfort"

# Extract substring
substr(sentence, 1, 12)

[1] "The patient "
Importantly, none of these operations require semantic understanding. They operate purely on symbolic structure. The computer is manipulating encoded numerical patterns, not meaning.
# Show position indexing

  position = seq_along(chars),
  character = chars
)

Indexing reveals another key property: computation requires ordered, addressable structure. Once language becomes a sequence that can be indexed, it becomes compatible with algorithms. This observation naturally leads to the scientific discipline of Natural Language Processing (NLP). NLP begins with the premise that language can be treated as structured numerical data and transformed into representations that support inference, learning, and prediction.
In other words:
Language → Numbers → Vectors → Probability Distributions → Learning
In the following sections, we move from raw strings to structured linguistic representations, and ultimately to probabilistic models capable of learning patterns from large corpora.

title: 10  Gen_AI Foundations I: Language as Computation
text:
10.2 What is Natural Language Processing?
Natural Language Processing (NLP) is the scientific and engineering discipline concerned with building computational systems that can work with human language. Its goal is to transform language—whether written text or speech—into representations that machines can manipulate, so that tasks such as classification, extraction, retrieval, translation, and generation become possible. In modern practice, NLP treats language as data: it can be measured, modeled, compressed, predicted, and generated. What makes NLP uniquely challenging is that language is not only a sequence of symbols, but also a vehicle for meaning, intent, and social context. As a result, NLP sits at the interface between formal structure (grammar and syntax), meaning (semantics), use in context (pragmatics), and the statistical patterns observed in very large collections of text and speech data—known as large corpora. A corpus is a structured collection of language data used for analysis or model training. Large corpora provide the empirical foundation for modern NLP systems, allowing computational models to estimate statistical regularities of grammar, vocabulary, and usage from real-world language. In contemporary language modeling, such corpora often contain billions of tokens drawn from diverse sources, enabling systems to generalize across domains and contexts. We will see what these terms mean in the following sections. These ideas are summarized in @fig-npl.






Figure 10.2: The diagram illustrates NLP as a central computational discipline connected to four foundational dimensions of language: grammar and syntax (formal structure), semantics (meaning representation), pragmatics (use in context), and large corpora (statistical patterns in data). Together, these components frame language as a structured, data-driven object that can be modeled and processed algorithmically.



The following code illustrates NLP by showing how a computer can scan human language and extract a useful information/signal from it—in this case, whether a sentence mentions “pain.” Even without understanding meaning like a human, simple text processing already enables practical language-based tasks such as screening, filtering, and routing information.

# NLP in one minute: making text actionable (no tokens yet)


# A tiny "corpus" (could be notes, emails, clinical snippets, etc.)
texts <- tibble(
  id = 1:4,
  text = c(
    "The patient reports chest pain and shortness of breath.",
    "No pain today. Symptoms improved after treatment.",
    "Please schedule a follow-up appointment next week.",
    "The trial report mentions adverse events and mild nausea."
  )
)

# Task: identify which lines mention pain (simple text-based decision)
results <- texts %>%
  mutate(
    mentions_pain = str_detect(str_to_lower(text), "\\bpain\\b")
  )

results

# A tibble: 4 × 3
     id text                                                      mentions_pain
  <int> <chr>                                                     <lgl>        
1     1 The patient reports chest pain and shortness of breath.   TRUE         
2     2 No pain today. Symptoms improved after treatment.         TRUE         
3     3 Please schedule a follow-up appointment next week.        FALSE        
4     4 The trial report mentions adverse events and mild nausea. FALSE        


In the following code we demonstrate a simple example on how to create a corpus in R. It begins by defining a small set of sentence templates containing placeholder variables such as {symptom}, {event}, {n}, and {unit}. These placeholders represent interchangeable linguistic elements. Separate vocabulary pools are then defined for each placeholder category—for example, a list of possible symptoms (“pain,” “nausea,” “fatigue”) and time units (“days,” “weeks”).
A helper function generates individual sentences by randomly selecting one template and replacing each placeholder with a randomly sampled value from its corresponding vocabulary pool. In this way, each generated sentence follows a coherent grammatical structure while varying in content. Repeating this process multiple times produces a collection of short, structured documents. These documents are stored in a tabular data frame (a tibble), where each row corresponds to a distinct text instance identified by a document identifier. This tabular organization makes the corpus easy to manipulate, filter, and analyze using standard data operations.

# A tiny corpus generator (simple + reusable)

set.seed(123)

# Sentence templates (very simple "grammar")
templates <- c(
  "The patient reports {symptom}.",
  "The patient denies {symptom}.",
  "Follow-up scheduled in {n} {unit}.",
  "The report mentions {event}.",
  "No {symptom} today; symptoms improved."
)

# Small vocab pools
symptoms <- c("pain", "nausea", "headache", "dizziness", "fatigue")
events   <- c("adverse events", "mild nausea", "elevated biomarkers", "improved response")
units    <- c("days", "weeks")

# Helper: fill one template with random values
make_sentence <- function() {
  t <- sample(templates, 1)
  t <- str_replace(t, "\\{symptom\\}", sample(symptoms, 1))
  t <- str_replace(t, "\\{event\\}",   sample(events, 1))
  t <- str_replace(t, "\\{n\\}",       as.character(sample(1:6, 1)))
  t <- str_replace(t, "\\{unit\\}",    sample(units, 1))
  t
}

# ------------------------------------------------------------
# 1) A corpus as a table (one row = one document)
# ------------------------------------------------------------
corpus_tbl <- tibble(
  doc_id = 1:12,
  text   = replicate(12, make_sentence())
)

corpus_tbl

# A tibble: 12 × 2
   doc_id text                                 
    <int> <chr>                                
 1      1 Follow-up scheduled in 2 weeks.      
 2      2 Follow-up scheduled in 6 weeks.      
 3      3 The patient reports nausea.          
 4      4 Follow-up scheduled in 1 days.       
 5      5 No headache today; symptoms improved.
 6      6 The patient denies pain.             
 7      7 The patient reports headache.        
 8      8 The patient denies fatigue.          
 9      9 The patient denies headache.         
10     10 No headache today; symptoms improved.
11     11 The patient denies fatigue.          
12     12 No nausea today; symptoms improved.  

# ------------------------------------------------------------
# 2) Split into two "sets of texts" (e.g., train/test)
# ------------------------------------------------------------
set.seed(123)
corpus_split <- corpus_tbl %>%
  mutate(set = if_else(runif(n()) < 0.7, "train", "test"))

train_texts <- corpus_split %>% filter(set == "train")
test_texts  <- corpus_split %>% filter(set == "test")

train_texts

# A tibble: 7 × 3
  doc_id text                                  set  
   <int> <chr>                                 <chr>
1      1 Follow-up scheduled in 2 weeks.       train
2      3 The patient reports nausea.           train
3      6 The patient denies pain.              train
4      7 The patient reports headache.         train
5      9 The patient denies headache.          train
6     10 No headache today; symptoms improved. train
7     12 No nausea today; symptoms improved.   train

test_texts

# A tibble: 5 × 3
  doc_id text                                  set  
   <int> <chr>                                 <chr>
1      2 Follow-up scheduled in 6 weeks.       test 
2      4 Follow-up scheduled in 1 days.        test 
3      5 No headache today; symptoms improved. test 
4      8 The patient denies fatigue.           test 
5     11 The patient denies fatigue.           test 


The steps above illustrates a common practice in computational language modeling: splitting the corpus into training and testing subsets. Each document is randomly assigned to either a “train” or “test” partition. The training subset is typically used to estimate model parameters, while the testing subset is reserved for evaluation. Even though this example is intentionally small and synthetic, it captures the essential idea that a corpus is not merely a collection of sentences, but a structured dataset prepared for systematic computational analysis and model development.
